The laser's applications now include surgery, manufacturing, communications, barcode scanners, and precision measurement.

Vaccines were pioneered by Edward Jenner in 1796, who observed that milkmaids who caught cowpox seemed immune to smallpox. He inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox pus, then exposed him to smallpox — the boy did not get sick. Jenner's word 'vaccine' (from Latin 'vacca,' cow) gave medicine its term for all immunizations.

The paper clip was patented by Norwegian inventor Johan Vaaler in 1899, though he lived in Germany where he filed the patent since Norway had no patent law. The Gem Manufacturing Company in Britain had produced a similar design even earlier without patenting it, and the 'Gem' clip became the dominant design used worldwide today.

The radio was developed by multiple inventors, with Guglielmo Marconi achieving the first transatlantic wireless transmission in 1901 and Nikola Tesla holding priority patents on core radio technologies. The US Supreme Court ruled in 1943 — after Marconi's death — that Tesla's patents predated Marconi's, partially restoring Tesla's legacy as a foundational inventor of radio.

The rubber eraser was an accidental discovery — Edward Nairne of England supposedly picked up a piece of rubber instead of breadcrumbs (the standard erasing tool) in 1770 and found it erased pencil marks perfectly. Joseph Priestley confirmed its use in writing and gave it the name 'rubber' because it rubbed out marks. Erasers were attached to pencils beginning in the 1850s.

The photocopier (xerography) was invented by Chester Carlson in a rented Queens, New York room in 1938, who was frustrated that there was no way to make quick copies of legal documents. After over 20 companies rejected his invention, the Haloid Company (later Xerox) licensed the patent in 1947 and commercialized the first office copier in 1959.

Thomas Edison filed more than 1,093 patents in the United States — a record that stood for decades. His Menlo Park laboratory, established in 1876, was effectively the world's first industrial research laboratory, with teams of engineers working systematically to develop commercially viable inventions, creating a model for corporate R&D that transformed the innovation ecosystem.

The intermittent windshield wiper was invented by Mary Anderson in 1903, a female entrepreneur from Alabama who noticed that streetcar drivers in New York had to stop constantly to clear sleet from their windows. She was unable to sell her patent and it expired in 1920 just as the automobile market exploded — making her invention one of history's most dramatic cases of an inventor losing out on patent timing.

Bluetooth wireless technology takes its name from 10th-century Danish King Harald 'Bluetooth' Blåtand, who united Scandinavian tribes — a metaphor for the technology uniting communication protocols. Developed by Ericsson engineer Jaap Haartsen in 1994 as a way to wirelessly connect mobile phones to headsets, it now connects billions of devices worldwide.

The screw propeller for ships was invented independently by Francis Pettit Smith in England and John Ericsson in Sweden in 1836. A pivotal 1845 trial called the 'Battle of the Propellers' pitted HMS Rattler (propeller) against HMS Alecto (paddle wheel) in a tug-of-war — Rattler towed Alecto backward at 2.5 knots, cementing the propeller's dominance.

Liquid crystal displays (LCDs) were first developed for practical use by George Heilmeier at RCA in 1968, though liquid crystals had been discovered in 1888 by Austrian botanist Friedrich Reinitzer. Modern LCDs are now in essentially every flat-screen TV, computer monitor, and smartphone, having displaced cathode ray tubes and becoming the world's dominant display technology.

The concrete reinforced by iron or steel rods was not invented by a single engineer but developed through parallel efforts in France by gardener Joseph Monier (flower pots, 1867) and contractor François Coignet (buildings, 1850s). German engineer G.A. Wayss systematized the structural engineering principles in the 1880s; reinforced concrete now accounts for more of the built environment by volume than any other material.

Braille was invented in 1824 by 15-year-old Louis Braille, who lost his sight in both eyes at age 3 in an accident at his father's workshop. Inspired by a military communication system of raised dots, Braille devised his own 6-dot code system that could be read by touch and written with a stylus — completing it at age 15 and revolutionizing literacy for the visually impaired.

The cotton mill powered by water — the first true factory — was built by Richard Arkwright at Cromford, England, in 1771. Arkwright's water frame produced strong cotton thread mechanically, and his factory system of organized labor working fixed shifts around machinery created the template for industrial production that transformed the global economy.

The internal combustion engine was developed by Nikolaus Otto in Germany in 1876, creating the four-stroke Otto cycle — intake, compression, power, exhaust — that is the basis for virtually all gasoline car engines today. Gottlieb Daimler and Karl Benz later adapted the engine for mobile use, with Benz patenting the first true automobile in January 1886.

The sewing machine was perfected for home and factory use by Isaac Singer in 1851, who invented the foot treadle, the presser foot, and a method for sewing continuously in straight or curved lines. Singer's company pioneered the installment payment plan to make sewing machines affordable, fundamentally changing how clothing was produced and creating one of the first major consumer finance industries.

The parachute was first successfully tested in free fall from a high-altitude balloon by André-Jacques Garnerin in 1797 over Paris. He designed a canopy based on an umbrella frame and descended from 900 meters — the chute oscillated wildly but he survived, immediately recognizing the problem of oscillation that was solved only in the 20th century with the central air vent.

The phonograph — the first device to record and reproduce sound — was invented by Thomas Edison in 1877 using a tinfoil cylinder. He was so confident it would not work that he barely believed the first playback of 'Mary Had a Little Lamb.' The gramophone disc (invented by Emile Berliner in 1887) replaced cylinders for music playback and became the dominant consumer audio format for nearly a century.

The first patent ever granted in the United States was issued on July 31, 1790 — Patent No. X1 — to Samuel Hopkins of Vermont for a new method of making potash (potassium carbonate) for use in soap and glass manufacturing. The patent was signed by President George Washington, Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson, and Attorney General Edmund Randolph.

Synthetic rubber was developed in Germany during World War I out of necessity when Allied blockades cut off natural rubber supplies. Bayer developed methyl rubber from dimethylbutadiene, and during World War II the USA and Germany raced to perfect synthetic rubber — the US Synthetic Rubber Program, one of the largest coordinated industrial efforts of the war, succeeded in time to prevent a strategic shortage.

The cat flap was reportedly invented by Isaac Newton, who — according to an apocryphal but widely repeated story — cut a large hole for his cat Spithead and a small hole for her kitten. What Newton may have actually invented is disputed, but the device that allows pets to pass through doors without human assistance has become ubiquitous in British homes.

The contraceptive pill was developed by chemist Carl Djerassi (who synthesized norethindrone in 1951) and biologist Gregory Pincus working with gynecologist John Rock in the USA, with the first clinical trials funded by feminist activist Margaret Sanger and heiress Katharine Dexter McCormick. The FDA approved it in 1960; Time magazine called it one of the 10 most important inventions of the 20th century.

The electric battery was invented by Alessandro Volta in 1800, who stacked alternating discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cardboard to create a 'voltaic pile' — the first device to produce a continuous, reliable electric current. Napoleon was so impressed that he made Volta a count; the unit of electric potential, the volt, is named in his honor.

The first programmable digital computer, ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), was built at the University of Pennsylvania and completed in 1945. The six women who operated and programmed ENIAC — Frances Bilas Spence, Jean Jennings Bartik, Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, Frances Bilas, and Betty Holberton — were largely unrecognized for decades and are now known as the 'ENIAC Women.'

The toaster was commercialized in 1909 by the General Electric Company with the D-12 model, the first safe electrical household appliance for consumers. The automatic pop-up toaster was invented by Charles Strite in 1919, frustrated that the cafeteria in his factory always burned the toast — he added a spring mechanism and adjustable timer to eject the toast automatically.

Wite-Out (correction fluid) was invented in 1956 by Bette Nesmith Graham, a secretary and single mother in Dallas, who thinned white tempera paint to brush over typing mistakes. She sold Liquid Paper from her kitchen and by 1975 was producing 25 million bottles a year, selling the company to Gillette for $47.5 million in 1979. Her son is musician Michael Nesmith of The Monkees.

The compact fluorescent lamp (CFL) was invented by Edward Hammer at General Electric in 1976 in response to the 1973 oil crisis and a demand for energy-efficient lighting. GE decided not to manufacture it due to the $25 million retooling cost; a decade later, Dutch company Philips commercialized an improved version, and CFLs eventually replaced incandescent bulbs in millions of homes worldwide.

Polaroid instant photography was invented by Edwin Land in 1947, inspired when his 3-year-old daughter asked why she couldn't see a photo immediately after it was taken. Land developed the complete self-developing film system in one afternoon's thinking in the early 1940s, and the Polaroid Land Model 95 camera, released in 1948, sold out before Christmas.

The nicotine patch was invented by Frank Etscorn, a psychology professor at New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, after he accidentally spilled nicotine solution on his hand and felt its effects transdermally. He patented the transdermal delivery device in 1985, though his invention was later licensed to pharmaceutical companies that refined and commercialized it.

Scotch tape (transparent cellophane tape) was invented by Richard Drew at 3M in 1930, following his earlier masking tape invention in 1925. When salesmen first brought samples to auto body shops during the Great Depression, workers discovered the tape was cheaper than proper paint, and Drew's invention became a global household product.

The airbag for automobiles was first patented by John Hetrick in 1952, inspired when a close car accident with his family made him wish for an instantaneous cushioning device. Despite his early patent, car manufacturers showed no interest for decades — GM's first production airbag appeared in 1973 and widespread mandatory adoption came only in the 1990s after millions of preventable deaths.

Kevlar fiber was licensed to DuPont in 1971, but Stephanie Kwolek received only a modest salary for her discovery — no royalties. Her case illustrates a recurring pattern in corporate R&D where female inventors at large companies frequently do not receive financial recognition matching their contributions, spurring debate about patent ownership and inventor compensation reforms.

Celluloid — the first industrial plastic, derived from cellulose nitrate — was invented by John Wesley Hyatt in 1869 as a substitute for ivory in billiard balls. While he never won the $10,000 prize offered for an ivory substitute, celluloid transformed manufacturing, becoming the basis for early photographic film, dental plates, and toys — and laid the groundwork for the modern plastics industry.

The carbon fiber composite material used in aircraft, Formula 1 cars, and sports equipment was developed at the Royal Aircraft Establishment in Farnborough, England, in 1963 by William Watt, Lessley Phillips, and William Johnson. The process of heating acrylic fibers (polyacrylonitrile) under tension transformed soft polymer strands into stiff graphite fibers eight times stronger than steel by weight.

The Jacquard loom — invented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in France in 1804 — used punched cards to control the weaving of complex patterns. This was the first programmable machine, and the punched card concept directly influenced Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine and eventually early computer punch-card systems used into the 1970s.

Freeze-dried food was developed to preserve blood plasma for military use during World War II, building on Clarence Birdseye's quick-freeze work. The coffee industry commercialized it after the war — Nescafé's instant freeze-dried coffee appeared in 1965 — and NASA later used freeze-drying extensively to supply astronauts with lightweight, shelf-stable food for space missions.

The fire sprinkler system was invented by Henry Parmelee in 1874, a piano manufacturer in New Haven, Connecticut, who wanted to protect his factory. His system used perforated pipes filled with water and sealed with plugs that melted at high temperature — a principle essentially unchanged in modern sprinklers that now protect billions of square meters of building space worldwide.

Corrugated cardboard was patented in 1871 by Albert Jones of New York for wrapping fragile bottles and glassware. The invention of the cardboard box in 1890 (by Robert Gair, also of New York) combined with corrugated cardboard to create the modern shipping box — which today holds together the global supply chain and is the single most used packaging material in the world.

The defibrillator was invented by Paul Zoll at Harvard in 1956, building on experiments by William Kouwenhoven and others in the 1940s. The automated external defibrillator (AED), developed in the 1970s, was designed for use by untrained bystanders and has been called the most important cardiac invention since the pacemaker — survival rates for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest double when an AED is used within 3 minutes.

The electric telegraph was preceded by optical telegraphy — Claude Chappe's semaphore tower network, built across France from 1793, transmitted messages via mechanical signals between towers visible with telescopes. Napoleon used it for military communications, and the system had about 534 stations covering 4,800 km by 1846, just before electric telegraphs made it obsolete.

The Bessemer converter, invented by Henry Bessemer in 1856, made steel production cheap and fast for the first time by blowing air through molten pig iron to burn off impurities. Within a decade, steel production costs fell by 80%, enabling the construction of railways, bridges, and skyscrapers that define the modern industrial world — but Bessemer was never awarded a knighthood despite his epoch-defining contribution.

Synthetic insulin was the first protein successfully produced by recombinant DNA technology when Genentech scientists in 1978 inserted the human insulin gene into E. coli bacteria, which then produced human insulin. FDA-approved in 1982 as Humulin, it replaced animal-derived insulin and inaugurated the modern biotechnology pharmaceutical industry.

The cochlear implant — an electronic device that directly stimulates the auditory nerve — was invented by Graeme Clark in Australia in the 1970s, who developed it to help his own deaf father. The first multi-channel cochlear implant was surgically implanted in 1978, and by 2022 over 700,000 people worldwide had received them, making it the most successful neural prosthesis in history.

The retractable ballpoint pen with a click mechanism was invented by László Bíró's brother György, who added a spring mechanism to the original pen. This refinement — so simple yet so satisfying — became one of the most-replicated product designs in history and is found in virtually every pen manufactured today.

The lie detector (polygraph) was developed by John Larson in 1921, building on physiological research by William Marston. The machine records blood pressure, pulse, respiration, and skin conductivity — but polygraph results have never been admitted as evidence in US federal courts because its accuracy is disputed. William Marston, the polygraph's co-inventor, also created the comic superhero Wonder Woman.

The 3D printer was invented by Chuck Hull in 1983 who developed stereolithography — using ultraviolet light to cure liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer. He founded 3D Systems in 1986 and filed the first 3D printing patent; the technology remained largely industrial until 2009 when the RepRap open-source project and expiring patents launched the desktop 3D printing revolution.

The electric motor was invented by Michael Faraday in 1821 — just one year after discovering electromagnetic rotation — when he demonstrated that a current-carrying wire would continuously rotate around a fixed magnet. His device was the first practical conversion of electrical to mechanical energy, and every electric motor from washing machines to Tesla cars descends from his principle.

Radar was invented independently in several countries in the 1930s, but Sir Robert Watson-Watt and his team developed the first practical early-warning radar system — Chain Home — deployed across Britain's coast by 1939. It was decisive in the Battle of Britain, giving the RAF enough warning to intercept Luftwaffe raids without exhausting pilots with permanent standing patrols.

The electric guitar was developed through contributions by several inventors, but George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker patented the first commercially successful electromagnetic pickup guitar in 1931 — the aluminum-bodied 'Frying Pan' lap steel guitar. Les Paul further revolutionized the solid-body electric guitar in 1941 with his homemade 'Log,' and the Gibson Les Paul became one of the iconic instruments of the 20th century.

Stainless steel was invented in 1913 by Harry Brearley, a British metallurgist in Sheffield who was testing alloys for gun barrels. He found that steel containing 12–13% chromium resisted acid and rust far better than regular steel — though initially dismissed, his alloy transformed cookware, cutlery, surgical instruments, and architecture.

The electric toothbrush was invented in 1954 by Philippe-Guy Woog in Switzerland as the Broxodent and was initially prescribed for patients with limited motor control. The cordless rechargeable Squibb Broxodent was introduced in the USA in 1960; today, dentists recommend electric toothbrushes as significantly more effective at plaque removal than manual brushing.

The global positioning of satellites in geosynchronous orbit was worked out by Arthur C. Clarke in 1945, predating actual satellites by 12 years. Clarke proposed in a Wireless World magazine article that three satellites positioned 120° apart at 35,786 km altitude would provide complete global coverage — the 'Clarke Orbit' is now named in his honor and contains thousands of operational satellites.

The smoke detector for residential use was developed in the 1960s by Donald Steele and Robert Emmons at Duane D. Pearsall's company SCI Systems. The first battery-powered home smoke detector was sold in 1965 for $125 — later mass production dropped prices dramatically. Smoke detectors have halved residential fire deaths in the USA since their widespread adoption in the 1970s.

The Internet (ARPANET) was developed by DARPA in the late 1960s under the direction of J.C.R. Licklider, Vint Cerf, and Bob Kahn. Cerf and Kahn invented TCP/IP in 1974 — the communication protocol that allowed different networks to interconnect — earning them the title 'Fathers of the Internet' and the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

The safety bicycle's direct evolutionary predecessor, the penny-farthing (or 'ordinary'), had front wheels up to 1.5 meters in diameter because the only way to go faster was a bigger front wheel — there were no gears. When John Kemp Starley introduced the chain drive in 1885, cyclists could use any wheel size and still vary their speed, making cycling safe and accessible for the first time.

Hydraulic engineering was pioneered in the 18th century by James Brindley and others, but the hydraulic press was invented by Joseph Bramah in 1795 using Pascal's law that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally throughout. The same principle underpins car brakes, industrial presses, and hydraulic excavators — all indirect descendants of Bramah's 1795 invention.

Breast cancer diagnostic mammography was developed in the 1960s by Robert Egan at M.D. Anderson Cancer Center, who standardized low-dose X-ray imaging of breast tissue. The National Breast Cancer Screening Program began in Sweden in 1977, and mammography screening has been credited with reducing breast cancer mortality by 20–40% in screened populations.

The disposable diaper was invented in 1948 by Marion Donovan, a housewife and Yale-trained architect who sewed a waterproof cover from a shower curtain and stuffed it with disposable absorbent material. The major manufacturers she approached rejected her design as unnecessary; she sold her patent for $1 million in 1951. Procter & Gamble later launched Pampers in 1961.

The wind turbine for generating electricity was built by Charles Brush in Cleveland in 1888 — a 60-foot-diameter 12-kilowatt machine that powered his mansion for 12 years. Danish scientist Poul la Cour later studied aerodynamics and efficiency in the 1890s and 1900s, establishing the engineering principles that underpin modern multi-megawatt wind turbines.

The microprocessor — the CPU on a single chip — was invented at Intel by engineers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stan Mazor, and the Intel 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, was released in November 1971. It had 2,300 transistors and ran at 0.74 MHz — less computing power than a modern digital wristwatch.

Toothpaste in its modern form was developed in the 1870s when Colgate began selling it in jars in 1873, and in collapsible tubes (an idea borrowed from artists' paint tubes) beginning in 1896. Fluoride toothpaste was developed in the 1950s, and its adoption is credited with a 30–60% reduction in childhood tooth decay in developed countries.

The photovoltaic solar cell was invented by Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, and Gerald Pearson at Bell Labs in 1954, producing electricity from sunlight with 6% efficiency. President Eisenhower's Science Advisory Committee called it one of the most significant inventions of the decade. The cost of solar electricity has fallen 99.6% since 1976, making solar the cheapest electricity source in history.

Modern air traffic control, using radio communication and radar to manage aircraft, was developed in the late 1930s. The first air traffic control center using radar was established at Indianapolis in 1956. Today, over 45,000 flights operate in US airspace daily — all coordinated by an invisible technological infrastructure invented over decades of iterative engineering.

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) were invented in 1928 by Thomas Midgley Jr. at General Motors as a safe, non-flammable refrigerant. His invention replaced toxic gases like ammonia and sulfur dioxide in refrigerators and was initially celebrated as an industrial miracle — only decades later did scientists discover CFCs were destroying the stratospheric ozone layer, leading to the 1987 Montreal Protocol ban.

The graphical user interface (GUI) was invented at Xerox PARC in the early 1970s by a team including Alan Kay and Larry Tesler, who developed windows, icons, menus, and the pointer concept (WIMP). Steve Jobs visited Xerox PARC in 1979, was shown the GUI, and incorporated it into the Apple Lisa and Macintosh — transforming personal computing from text command systems to the visual interface used worldwide today.

The detonating blasting cap was invented by Alfred Nobel in 1864, solving the problem of reliably and safely detonating nitroglycerin from a distance. Before it, miners had to use open flames near highly sensitive explosives — with lethal results. The blasting cap, combined with his later dynamite invention, made Nobel the most significant mining engineer of his era.

The jukebox — an automatic coin-operated record player — first appeared in 1889 as the 'Nickel-in-the-Slot' machine at the Palais Royale Saloon in San Francisco. The Wurlitzer Company's Model 750, introduced in 1941 with its iconic illuminated bubble tubes and colorful cabinet, became the definitive jukebox design and one of the most recognized industrial designs of the 20th century.

The combine harvester — which cuts, threshes, and separates grain in a single pass — was patented by Hiram Moore in Michigan in 1835. Steam-powered combines appeared in the 1880s, and modern GPS-guided combines can harvest over 100 acres per day. A single modern combine does the work that would have required 150 harvesters working a full day by hand.

The first programmable general-purpose computer, Colossus, was designed by Tommy Flowers and built at the UK's Post Office Research Station in 1943 to crack German Lorenz cipher machine messages at Bletchley Park. Winston Churchill ordered all 10 Colossus machines destroyed after the war and the project kept secret until the 1970s — delaying recognition of British computer pioneers for decades.

The retinal scan biometric identification system was patented by Leonard Flom and Aran Safir in 1987, with the algorithm developed by John Daugman in 1993. Iris recognition exploits the fact that the iris pattern is essentially random, highly individual, and stable throughout a person's lifetime — making it more reliable than fingerprints and now used in airports and border crossings worldwide.

The hydraulic turbine for generating electricity at scale was perfected by James Francis in Lowell, Massachusetts in 1849 — the Francis turbine is still the most widely used water turbine worldwide and generates more hydroelectric power than any other design. The Hoover Dam uses Francis turbines, as do the Three Gorges Dam and the majority of the world's hydroelectric capacity.

Nitroglycerin was synthesized by Italian chemist Ascanio Sobrero in 1847, who was so horrified by its explosive power that he initially tried to keep it secret. He warned his former student Alfred Nobel against using it — but Nobel went on to develop it into commercial dynamite and blasting caps. Sobrero received essentially no credit or compensation while Nobel became one of the wealthiest industrialists in Europe.

The paracetamol (acetaminophen) pain reliever was first synthesized in 1877 but was largely overlooked in favor of aspirin; it was rediscovered and tested at Johns Hopkins in 1948. Paracetamol became one of the most widely used analgesics in the world, sold as Tylenol in the USA and Panadol in much of the world — but its therapeutic window is narrow, and overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure in developed countries.

The polio vaccine was developed by Jonas Salk in 1952 and field-tested in 1954 in the largest public health experiment in history — involving 1.8 million children known as 'Polio Pioneers.' Salk refused to patent the vaccine, stating 'there is no patent; could you patent the sun?' His choice made the vaccine immediately available worldwide and gave him legendary status.

The jet engine was independently invented by Frank Whittle in England and Hans von Ohain in Germany in the 1930s; Whittle patented his design in 1930 but the British Air Ministry showed no interest for years, while Ohain's engine powered the first jet aircraft flight (He 178) on August 27, 1939. Whittle's engine powered the first British jet, the Gloster E.28/39, in 1941.

Linoleum flooring was invented in 1863 by British rubber merchant Frederick Walton, who noticed that oxidized linseed oil formed a tough, flexible skin on paint tins. He developed a process to coat hessian canvas with this material and patented the name 'linoleum' from the Latin for linseed oil. Victorian and Edwardian linoleum was cheaper and more hygienic than wooden floors and transformed working-class domestic interiors.

The metal detector was invented by Alexander Graham Bell in 1881, urgently designed to locate the bullet lodged in President James Garfield after his assassination attempt. The device worked in testing but failed to locate the bullet in Garfield — later determined to be because the metal springs in his mattress interfered with the signal. Garfield died from infection rather than the bullet itself.

Play-Doh was invented by Noah McVicker in 1956 as a wallpaper cleaning compound — a non-toxic putty to clean coal soot from wallpaper. When a nursery school teacher realized children preferred it to modeling clay, McVicker rebranded the product, added colors, and sold it as a toy. Within a year of its toy launch, over 3 million cans were sold.

The first practical typewriter was patented in 1868 by Christopher Latham Sholes, Carlos Glidden, and Samuel Soulé in Milwaukee. Sholes later designed the QWERTY keyboard layout, reportedly to separate commonly used letter pairs and reduce jamming. Sholes sold his patents to Remington & Sons for $12,000 — declining a royalty deal that would have made him one of the wealthiest men in America.

The sports bra was invented by Hinda Miller and Lisa Lindahl in 1977, who sewed two jockstraps together as a prototype. Nicknamed the 'jockbra,' it was the first athletic garment specifically designed for women's physiology. Before the sports bra, women exercised in modified regular bras or went without — and many physicians claimed vigorous physical activity was harmful to women.

The neon sign was developed by French engineer Georges Claude, who demonstrated neon-filled glass tubes glowing red at the Paris Motor Show in 1910. He sold the first US neon signs to a Los Angeles Packard car dealership in 1923 for $1,250 each; passersby reportedly stopped and stared for 30 minutes. At peak use in the 1960s, neon signs were the dominant form of commercial advertising lighting.

The flushing toilet is often attributed to Thomas Crapper — largely a myth, though Crapper was a plumber who popularized its use — but the first water closet with a flushing valve was designed by Alexander Cumming in 1775 and improved by Joseph Bramah in 1778. Modern sanitation infrastructure based on flushing toilets is estimated to have saved more lives than any other engineering invention.

Superalloys — heat-resistant metallic alloys based on nickel, cobalt, or iron — were first developed in the 1940s for jet engine turbine blades. Modern superalloys can operate at temperatures above their own melting point when cooled by internal air channels, and their continuous improvement has been a key driver of jet engine efficiency — a single turbine blade in a modern engine is one of the most technically complex metal objects ever manufactured.

The MRI contrast agent gadolinium chelate was developed in the 1980s, significantly improving the diagnostic capability of MRI by highlighting tumors and lesions. Its development is a case study in how incremental pharmaceutical innovation — building on an imaging technology invented a decade earlier — can dramatically change clinical medicine.

The first commercial fiber optic communication link was installed in Long Beach, California, in 1977 by AT&T and General Telephone, carrying telephone calls using glass fibers instead of copper wire. Fiber optic cables now carry virtually all international internet traffic — the global fiber optic cable network is over 1.2 million kilometers long, circumnavigating Earth about 30 times.

The shopping cart was invented by Sylvan Goldman in 1937 at his Standard Food Store in Oklahoma City; he noticed customers stopped shopping when their handheld baskets got too heavy. His first carts, featuring a folding chair frame with baskets, were initially rejected by shoppers who found them embarrassing — he hired models of all ages to push them around his store to demonstrate normalcy.

The first programmable electronic calculator, the HP-35, was introduced by Hewlett-Packard in 1972 at a price of $395 — a year's worth of scientific calculation work in a shirt-pocket device. It was named the HP-35 because it had 35 keys; HP engineers calculated it was impossible and called it 'Hewlett's Folly' — until it sold 300,000 units in its first year.

Sunscreen was invented in 1936 by chemist Eugène Schueller, founder of L'Oréal, using benzyl cinnamate and benzyl salicylate to absorb UV rays. The SPF (Sun Protection Factor) rating system was developed by Franz Greiter in 1974 — he had originally invented his Glacier Cream after getting sunburned while climbing Piz Buin in the Alps in 1938.

The mechanical clock with an escapement — a device that controls the transfer of energy and keeps time — was invented in medieval Europe around 1275–1300, with the first public mechanical clocks appearing in Italian cities around 1300. This invention separated timekeeping from celestial observation, made precise coordination of human activity possible, and is arguably a foundation of modern industrial civilization.

The airliner pressurized cabin was first used commercially by Boeing on the Model 307 Stratoliner in 1940, which could fly above weather and turbulence at 6,100 meters. Before cabin pressurization, commercial airliners flew low enough that passengers needed oxygen masks above 3,000 meters, severely limiting speed and altitude. Pressurization transformed aviation from an adventure to mass transportation.

The catalytic converter for automobiles was invented by French engineer Eugene Houdry, who patented the design in 1950 motivated by his alarm at smog in Los Angeles. The device oxidizes carbon monoxide and hydrocarbons to carbon dioxide and water, and reduces nitrogen oxides to nitrogen. Mandatory in US cars since 1975, catalytic converters have reduced urban air pollution by 70–90% relative to 1970 levels.

The first commercial nuclear power plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union, which began generating electricity on June 27, 1954. The USA opened Shippingport Atomic Power Station in 1958 as the first large-scale civilian nuclear power plant in the Western world; today, nuclear power produces about 10% of global electricity with the lowest lifecycle carbon emissions of any power source.

The LED (light-emitting diode) was first demonstrated producing visible light by Nick Holonyak Jr. at General Electric in 1962. His red LED was initially used only as indicator lights; the blue LED — invented by Shuji Nakamura, Hiroshi Amano, and Isamu Akasaki in 1994 — enabled white LED lighting and earned them the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics for enabling the energy-efficient lighting revolution.

The Segway personal transporter was invented by Dean Kamen and unveiled in 2001 after enormous pre-release hype — Steve Jobs reportedly called it 'as big a deal as the PC.' Despite this, Segways sold only 30,000 units in five years, far short of expectations, making it one of the most famous examples of an invention that worked technically but failed to find a mass market.

Gorilla Glass — the thin, tough aluminosilicate glass used in virtually all smartphone screens — was invented by Corning in 1962 as 'Project Muscle' but was shelved because no market existed. When Steve Jobs called Corning CEO Wendell Weeks in 2006 asking for large quantities in six months, Corning resurrected the 44-year-old glass formula, and Gorilla Glass now protects over 8 billion devices.

The barcode was invented by Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver in 1949, inspired when Woodland drew Morse code dots and dashes in sand at a beach and then extended them into concentric circles. The first product scanned with a barcode at retail — on June 26, 1974 — was a 10-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio.

The first patent for a method of birth control was held by an African-American inventor — Otis Boykin, who did not invent birth control but did hold 26 patents including the resistor used in pacemakers. The broader story of Black inventors in the USA is marked by barriers to patent filing under slavery and segregation — yet enslaved inventor Ned invented an improved cotton scraper in 1857 but could not hold a patent under law.

Bakelite — the first fully synthetic plastic made from fossil fuel chemicals — was invented by Belgian-American chemist Leo Baekeland in 1907 by reacting phenol with formaldehyde under heat and pressure. Bakelite could be molded when heated and then permanently hardened, making it the first thermosetting plastic and the first plastic used in mass production of consumer goods.

Sign language as a formal structured language was codified by Abbé Charles-Michel de l'Épée in Paris in the 1770s, who observed deaf children using signs to communicate and systematized it into French Sign Language. Deaf student Laurent Clerc brought this system to the USA in 1817, co-founding the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, Connecticut, with Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet.

The pneumatic tire was invented by Scottish veterinarian John Boyd Dunlop in 1887 when he fitted air-filled rubber tubes to his son's tricycle to give a smoother ride. He had no idea that Robert William Thomson had patented essentially the same invention in 1845 and been ignored for 40 years; Dunlop's patent was later declared invalid but his company thrived as the Dunlop Rubber Company.

Cholera mapping and the concept of epidemiology as a tool for understanding disease transmission were pioneered by John Snow in 1854 using a manual map. By plotting cases of the Soho cholera outbreak on a street map, he identified the Broad Street pump as the source — a method now recognized as the founding of modern epidemiology and evidence-based public health policy.

The postal system as a state institution was invented by Cyrus the Great of Persia around 550 BCE, using relay stations with fresh horses every 25 kilometers — the first rapid communication network. Herodotus described the Persian couriers as stopped by 'neither snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night,' a phrase still carved on the New York City Post Office.

Bioprinting — using a 3D printer to deposit living cells layer by layer into biological structures — was pioneered by Thomas Boland at Clemson University in 2003, who modified an inkjet printer to dispense cells instead of ink. Researchers have since bioprinted skin, cartilage, and vascular tissue, and the first 3D-printed organ transplanted into a human (a trachea) was performed in 2011.

The first commercially successful steam locomotive, the Rocket, was built by George and Robert Stephenson and won the 1829 Rainhill Trials, reaching 47 km/h. The Rocket's multi-tube boiler — which dramatically increased steam production efficiency over single-flue designs — was a key innovation that made practical steam railways possible and launched the railway age.

The AK-47 assault rifle was designed in 1947 by Mikhail Kalashnikov, a Soviet sergeant who had been wounded in battle and wanted to create a reliable weapon for Russian infantry. With over 100 million units manufactured, it is the most produced firearm in history — and its simplicity, durability, and ease of repair have made it the weapon of choice in conflicts worldwide for 75 years.

The first email was sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson of BBN Technologies, who chose the '@' symbol to separate user names from host computers. Tomlinson sent test messages to himself on two adjacent computers — he later said he had no idea what he sent and considered it 'not a significant invention.' Email now accounts for over 300 billion messages sent per day.

The safety pin can be traced far back in history — ancient fibulae used by Greeks and Romans were functionally identical. The modern coiled safety pin was the specific invention of Walter Hunt in 1849, but the concept of a pin with a protective clasp has been independently invented across cultures for over 2,500 years, making it one of the most multiply-invented objects in human history.

Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) for natural gas was commercially developed by Halliburton in 1949, but the technique that enabled the modern shale gas boom was invented by George Mitchell in the 1990s, combining horizontal drilling with high-volume hydraulic fracturing to extract gas from tight shale formations. This technique transformed the USA from a gas importer to the world's largest natural gas producer.

The modern condom was developed in vulcanized rubber by American Charles Goodyear and English Charles Hancock in the 1840s, but the latex condom — far thinner, stronger, and more comfortable — was manufactured from 1919 onwards. The female condom was invented by Lasse Hessel in Denmark in 1984 and introduced commercially in 1993 — it remains underutilized despite giving women autonomous contraceptive control.

The plow, one of humanity's most transformative inventions, was developed around 4000–3500 BCE in Mesopotamia and ancient China. The moldboard plow — which turns the soil over rather than just scratching it — was developed in China around 200 BCE and independently in medieval Europe around the 7th century CE, enabling farming of heavy, waterlogged northern European soils and feeding much denser populations.

The Lunar Rover used during Apollo 15, 16, and 17 was designed by Boeing and built by GM's Delco Electronics in just 17 months between 1969 and 1971. The battery-powered vehicle weighed only 210 kg and allowed astronauts to travel up to 7.6 km from their landing site, expanding the geological survey capability of each mission enormously. The three rovers remain on the Moon today.

The water wheel — one of the first machines to harness natural energy — was described by Roman engineer Vitruvius around 25 BCE and is likely much older. Medieval European water mills ground grain, powered bellows, sawed timber, and hammered metal; by the 11th century, England had over 5,000 water mills as recorded in the Domesday Book, making water power the backbone of medieval industrial production.

The Hyperloop concept — a pneumatic tube transportation system for passengers traveling in sealed pods at near-supersonic speed — was proposed by Elon Musk in a 2013 white paper. Multiple companies attempted to develop it in the 2010s, but by the mid-2020s all major commercial Hyperloop ventures had folded due to engineering and financial challenges, making it one of the most prominent failed invention attempts of the era.

Freeze-dried coffee — the most convenient form of instant coffee — is a distinct invention from instant coffee powder, which was created by Satori Kato, a Japanese-American chemist, in 1903. George Constant Louis Washington commercialized it in 1910, and G. Washington Coffee was the first commercial instant coffee brand, supplied to the US Army in World War I.

The mechanical reaper — enabling one person to harvest grain as fast as several by hand — was invented by Cyrus McCormick in 1831 and patented in 1834. McCormick's reaper and its descendants are credited with enabling the expansion of grain farming across the American Midwest, feeding rapidly growing industrial cities and transforming the USA into the world's breadbasket.

The voltaic pile — the first electric battery — could not sustain current for long, but within a year of Volta's 1800 announcement, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle used it to perform the first electrolysis of water, splitting it into hydrogen and oxygen. This set the stage for electrochemistry as a field and eventually for hydrogen fuel cells two centuries later.

The Pill camera — a swallowable capsule containing a tiny camera that photographs the entire gastrointestinal tract — was invented by Israeli engineer Gavriel Iddan in the 1990s and approved by the FDA in 2001 as the PillCam. Before its introduction, the small intestine was largely inaccessible to endoscopy; the PillCam images the entire 6-meter intestinal tract in 8 hours as it passes through naturally.

Robert Goddard launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926, from a farm in Auburn, Massachusetts. His rocket reached an altitude of 12.5 meters and traveled 56 meters in 2.5 seconds — mocked by The New York Times as proof that rockets couldn't work in a vacuum (the paper issued a correction 49 years later, the day before Apollo 11 launched).

Flow meters for measuring gas or liquid flow through pipes were first developed in the late 19th century, but the ultrasonic flow meter — which uses sound waves rather than mechanical parts — was invented by Shigeo Satomura in Japan in 1956. Modern transit-time ultrasonic meters have no moving parts, require no pipe cutting, and measure flow non-invasively from outside the pipe.

The crossbow was invented independently in China around 600 BCE and in the Mediterranean around the same time. In medieval Europe, the steel-bowed crossbow could penetrate armor that arrows could not, making it so feared that the Second Lateran Council in 1139 banned it for use against Christians — a ruling completely ignored by all parties in subsequent wars.

Wearable heart monitors were pioneered by Norman Holter in 1949, who invented the portable electrocardiogram recorder (Holter monitor) that records heart activity over 24–48 hours during normal daily activities. Named after Holter, these devices have been used in billions of diagnostic recordings and remain the standard tool for detecting arrhythmias that are intermittent and missed by standard ECG.

The water pump driven by Archimedes' screw principle is attributed to Archimedes of Syracuse around 250 BCE, though similar devices may have been used in ancient Egypt. The screw pump lifts water by rotating a helical screw inside a cylinder — modern applications include wastewater treatment, flood drainage, and fish ladders. The world's largest Archimedes' screw pumps are used to drain polders in the Netherlands.

The polygraph machine has a direct descendant in the fMRI lie detector, which measures brain activity to detect deception. Neither device is accepted as legally admissible evidence in most jurisdictions, but both illustrate how inventors continuously attempt to create technology to detect truth — a goal that has fascinated inventors from Cesare Lombroso's 1895 heart rate monitor to modern AI behavioral analysis.

The wristwatch was developed for women as a fashionable bracelet watch in the late 19th century, while men continued using pocket watches. It transitioned to military use in World War I — synchronized wristwatch timing of artillery barrages was critical to coordinated infantry attacks. After the war, returning soldiers kept their wristwatches, and men's pocket watches became obsolete within a decade.

Margarine was invented in 1869 by French chemist Hippolyte Mège-Mouriès, who won a competition set by Napoleon III to find a cheap butter substitute for soldiers and the poor. He emulsified beef tallow with milk and called it 'oleomargarine'; later versions used vegetable oils, and today margarine production is a multi-billion-dollar global industry — though its reputation has suffered from the trans fat controversy.

The hearing aid traces its origins to the ear trumpet — a hand-held funnel used since the 17th century. The first electric hearing aid was built by Miller Reese Hutchison in 1898 using a carbon microphone and battery. Transistor-based hearing aids appeared in 1952, and modern digital behind-the-ear hearing aids can separate speech from background noise and stream audio from smartphones wirelessly.

Hydraulic cement — a cement that hardens underwater — was rediscovered in the 18th century by John Smeaton while rebuilding the Eddystone Lighthouse in 1756. The Romans had used a similar volcanic ash-based cement (pozzolana) for their harbor structures, but the technology had been lost. Smeaton's work led directly to the development of Portland cement by Joseph Aspdin in 1824.

The wind-up music box was invented in Geneva, Switzerland around 1796 by Antoine Favre, a watchmaker who used a tuned steel comb plucked by pins on a rotating cylinder. The music box industry flourished in Switzerland through the 19th century, employing thousands; it was displaced by the phonograph in the 1890s. The Swiss music box tradition directly influenced the development of early sound-producing mechanisms in toys.

Cat litter was invented by Ed Lowe in 1947 when a neighbor asked if he had sand for her cat's box. Lowe offered her granulated clay (kiln-dried fuller's earth) used in industrial absorbents — she came back for more. He called the product Kitty Litter and sold it from his car, eventually building a $200 million company. The invention transformed cats from outdoor animals to the world's most popular indoor pets.

Semaphore communication — using flags or paddles in specific positions to encode letters — was standardized for maritime use in the early 19th century and remains in use as an emergency backup for naval communication. The more famous optical semaphore, Claude Chappe's tower network, inspired the visual language used in railway signaling, which in turn established conventions later adapted for electronic telegraphic codes.

The iron lung — a negative-pressure ventilator that encases the patient's body and draws air into paralyzed lungs by creating alternating pressure — was invented by Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw at Harvard in 1927. During polio epidemics of the 1940s and 1950s, iron lungs kept thousands of patients alive; some patients spent decades inside them, and a handful were still using them in the 21st century.

The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by Hungarian architecture professor Ernő Rubik, who created it as a teaching tool to help his students understand three-dimensional geometry. He spent a month solving it himself after creating it, not initially sure it could be solved. With over 450 million sold, the Rubik's Cube is the best-selling puzzle toy in history.

The gas turbine engine for industrial power generation was first successfully run by Swiss company Brown Boveri in 1939 — producing 4 MW in Neuchâtel and still operating today as the world's oldest gas turbine. Modern gas turbines are the most thermally efficient single-cycle heat engines ever built, converting up to 46% of fuel energy into electricity.

The synthetic plastics that have been most revolutionary in medicine include silicone — developed by Frederick Kipping in England in the 1940s — which is used in implants, catheters, and medical tubing. Dow Corning commercialized silicone for medical use in the 1940s, and today silicone elastomers are used in cardiac valves, joint replacements, and drug delivery systems.

Flash memory — the storage technology in USB drives, SSDs, and smartphone memory — was invented by Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba in 1984. He presented it at a conference without his employer's permission; Intel recognized its potential, commercialized it aggressively, and became a dominant manufacturer. Masuoka received a small bonus from Toshiba for one of the most commercially valuable semiconductor inventions of the 20th century.

The personal jet pack — a wearable rocket device that lifts a person off the ground — was first demonstrated by Wendell Moore at Bell Aerosystems in 1961. Despite decades of development, the Bell Rocket Belt could only fly for 21 seconds due to fuel constraints. Modern hydrogen peroxide and turbine-powered jet suits by companies like Gravity Industries have extended flight times to minutes, but practical commuter jet packs remain decades away.

The modern syringe driver — a programmable device that slowly delivers precise drug doses over hours — was invented by R.A. Parker and S.M. Skeggs at Becton Dickinson in 1954 for chemotherapy. Syringe drivers now allow terminally ill patients to receive continuous pain medication at home without IV lines, transforming palliative care and making comfortable death at home possible for millions.

Artificial intelligence as a field was formally established in 1956 at the Dartmouth Conference organized by John McCarthy, who coined the term 'artificial intelligence.' McCarthy also invented the LISP programming language in 1958, which remained the standard AI programming language for decades. The field has since experienced multiple cycles of enthusiasm and 'AI winters' before the deep learning revolution of the 2010s.

Chloroform was first used as a surgical anesthetic in 1847 by Scottish obstetrician James Young Simpson, who tested it on himself and his colleagues at a dinner party before using it clinically. Queen Victoria used chloroform during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, ending the religious argument that labor pain was divinely ordained and should not be relieved.

Noise-cancelling headphones were invented by Dr. Amar Bose in 1978 after wearing uncomfortable airline headsets on a long flight — he sketched the first concept on his flight napkin. His idea was to sample the ambient noise with a microphone and create an inverted 'anti-noise' signal to cancel it; Bose Corporation commercialized the first aviation headset in 1989 and consumer version in 2000.

The gyroscope was invented as a scientific instrument by Léon Foucault in 1852, who used it to demonstrate Earth's rotation. Its property of maintaining a fixed orientation in space regardless of the frame around it makes it essential for navigation — gyroscopes guided Apollo spacecraft to the Moon and are still used in aircraft, submarines, and smartphones for orientation sensing.

The modern prosthetic limb dates to the Civil War, when battlefield amputations created an unprecedented demand for functional artificial limbs. Surgeon General William Hammond commissioned a research program that led to the 'American Leg' patented in 1863 — notable for using rubber bumpers to simulate tendon spring. Today's myoelectric prosthetics read muscle electrical signals to control motorized joints with extraordinary precision.

Spectacles (eyeglasses) were invented in Italy around 1290, with Pisa and Venice competing for credit. The earliest glasses corrected only farsightedness; lenses for myopia (nearsightedness) weren't developed until about 1450. Before glasses, learned monks whose vision deteriorated in their 40s could no longer read or copy manuscripts — glasses literally extended the productive scholarly life by decades.

The Enigma cipher machine, used by Nazi Germany, was a rotor-based electromechanical encryption device invented by Arthur Scherbius in 1918 for commercial banking communications. The German military adopted and enhanced it in the 1920s–30s; its ciphers were broken by Polish mathematicians (Marian Rejewski, Jerzy Różycki, and Henryk Zygalski) in 1932 and by Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park in 1941.

The artificial hip joint replacement was pioneered by John Charnley at Wrightington Hospital in Lancashire in the early 1960s using a metal femoral head articulating against a polyethylene socket cemented in place with acrylic bone cement. Charnley's low-friction arthroplasty became the standard procedure worldwide and has restored mobility to over 10 million people.

The can of soda (carbonated beverage) was first sold commercially by Clicquot Club ginger ale in 1938, though the crown bottle cap had been available since 1892. The pull-tab opener was invented by Ermal Fraze in 1959 after forgetting his church key at a picnic; his ring-pull design is the basis for every modern easy-open can lid.

The mechanical pencil (propelling pencil) was patented in 1822 by Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in England, featuring a screw-advance mechanism. Modern mechanical pencils use a collet chuck to grip and advance thin 0.3–0.9 mm polymer-bonded graphite leads — a precision manufacturing achievement that makes them the writing instruments of choice for engineers, architects, and test-takers worldwide.

Magnetic stripe card technology — the black stripe on credit and ID cards — was invented by IBM engineer Forrest Parry in 1960. Parry attempted unsuccessfully to glue magnetic tape to a card; his wife suggested using a household iron. The resulting magnetic stripe card became the universal standard for banking, transit, and access control for over 50 years before chip-and-PIN and contactless technology began replacing it.

The cotton candy machine was co-invented by dentist William Morrison and confectioner John C. Wharton, who patented the electric candy machine in 1897 and introduced it at the 1897 Tennessee Centennial Exposition as 'Fairy Floss.' One of history's most ironic inventions — candy marketed partly by a dentist — cotton candy remains one of the most popular fairground foods worldwide.

The parking meter was invented by Carl Magee in Oklahoma City and the first was installed on July 16, 1935. Magee designed it as a solution to downtown congestion caused by all-day parkers; it was controversial from the start — the Oklahoma Supreme Court initially ruled it illegal — but spread worldwide and became both a revenue source and urban planning tool.

Insulin pump therapy — delivering continuous subcutaneous insulin via a wearable pump — was pioneered by Arnold Kadish in 1963 and refined by Dean Kamen (who also invented the Segway) in 1973. Modern insulin pumps store days of insulin in a cartridge and communicate with continuous glucose monitors to automatically adjust delivery — the 'closed-loop' artificial pancreas that dramatically improves quality of life for Type 1 diabetics.

The disposable lighter was mass-marketed by Bic in France in 1973, though the technology — a flint and gas mechanism — had been in use since the 1820s. The Bic lighter is manufactured with tolerances so tight that it works reliably in conditions from −25°C to 50°C; over 8 billion have been sold, making it one of the most universally distributed manufactured objects in history.

The CAT scan (computed axial tomography) was invented by Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI in England and Allan Cormack in South Africa working independently; both shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The first clinical CT scanner was installed at Atkinson Morley Hospital in London in 1971; it took 9 days of computer processing to produce a single cross-sectional image.

The mechanical loom is credited in its power-driven form to Edmund Cartwright, who patented the power loom in 1785 despite having no textile knowledge — he was a clergyman. His first machine was so poorly designed it could not be used, but after working with smiths and engineers he produced a functional model; it threatened handloom weavers, who rioted and burned his factories.

The crossword puzzle was invented by Arthur Wynne, a journalist from Liverpool, who published the first one in the New York World on December 21, 1913. He called it a 'word-cross' and it was a diamond shape rather than a grid; the modern rectangular grid format became standard in the 1920s, and the New York Times first published a crossword in 1942 after years of editorial opposition.

The modern food processor was invented in France by Pierre Verdun in 1960; his Robot-Coupe commercial machine automated chopping, slicing, and shredding in professional kitchens. Cuisinart introduced the home version in the USA in 1973 after Carl Sontheimer saw the Robot-Coupe at a trade fair and redesigned it for domestic use, bringing restaurant-quality food preparation into the home kitchen.

Hydraulic cement and Roman concrete (opus caementicium) used volcanic ash (pozzolana) mixed with seawater and lime to create a material that hardened underwater and continued to strengthen over centuries. Modern analysis has revealed that Roman harbor concrete is stronger after 2,000 years than when first made — a property modern Portland cement does not share — inspiring 21st-century research into more durable and sustainable cements.

The first contraceptive was reportedly a mixture of crocodile dung, honey, and natron (soda) used as a pessary in ancient Egypt around 1850 BCE, described in the Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus. While its effectiveness was likely limited, it represents the oldest documented attempt to prevent pregnancy — illustrating that reproductive control has been a human concern for nearly four millennia.

Angiography — X-ray imaging of blood vessels using injected contrast dye — was invented by Egas Moniz in Portugal in 1927, initially to diagnose brain tumors by imaging cerebral blood vessels. Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine — controversial because the prize citation was for lobotomy, not angiography, which proved the more durable contribution to medicine.

The portable calculator was preceded by the slide rule, invented by William Oughtred in 1622 as an analog computing device that multiplied and divided by adding and subtracting logarithms. For 350 years, the slide rule was the primary computational tool for engineers, scientists, and navigators — the Apollo astronauts carried backup slide rules to the Moon — before being replaced within a decade by pocket calculators in the early 1970s.

The Walkman personal cassette player was invented by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita of Sony, released in Japan on July 1, 1979. When Sony's marketing department predicted sales of 5,000 units per month, Morita said they would sell 10,000 — actual sales were 50,000 in the first two months. The Walkman redefined how and where people listened to music and popularized personal audio for the first time.

The tampon was invented by American physician Earle Haas in 1929 and patented in 1931, though he had no commercial success and sold the patent for $32. Gertrude Tendrich purchased the patent, founded Tampax, and created the first commercial tampon product — making the company's success the result of a woman entrepreneur commercializing a medical invention overlooked by its male inventor.

Tetanus toxoid vaccine was developed in the 1920s by French immunologists Gaston Ramon and Christian Ehrlich at the Pasteur Institute. Prior to vaccination, tetanus was a common killer of battlefield wounded and newborns. The vaccine essentially eliminated neonatal tetanus from vaccinated populations — yet globally, tens of thousands of newborns still die from tetanus annually in regions with low vaccination coverage.

The wired telegraph led directly to wireless telegraphy (radio), which led to broadcast radio, which led to television — each medium being an incremental extension of the fundamental idea that information can be encoded in electromagnetic signals. Philo Farnsworth, an Idaho farm boy, transmitted the first fully electronic television image in September 1927 at age 21 — a horizontal line — patenting a system that outperformed RCA's competing mechanical television.

The QR code was invented by Masahiro Hara of Denso Wave in Japan in 1994, designed to track automotive parts in Toyota's factories. Denso Wave intentionally did not enforce its patent, making QR codes freely available — a decision that enabled the global adoption that turned them from a niche industrial tool into the universal mobile payment, information, and authentication platform they are today.

Freeze drying of vaccines and biologics was developed in the 1940s, enabling stable storage and transport of fragile medical products without refrigeration. This innovation — applying a technology developed for blood plasma to vaccines — was critical to global vaccination campaigns: the smallpox eradication program required freeze-dried vaccine that could be stored and used in remote areas without cold chains.

The lawn mower was invented by Edwin Budding in Stroud, England, in 1830, adapting a textile mill cutting machine to trim grass uniformly. Before the lawnmower, grass in formal gardens was cut by scythe-wielding gangs — expensive work restricted to wealthy estates. Budding's machine made the manicured lawn accessible to the middle class and created the distinctly British obsession with the garden lawn.

The integrated circuit was invented simultaneously and independently by Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1958–1959. Kilby received the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for his invention (Noyce had died in 1990 and Nobel Prizes are not awarded posthumously). The integrated circuit enabled the miniaturization that makes all modern electronics possible.

The ice cream cone was popularized (and possibly invented) at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair when Ernest Hamwi, a Syrian waffle vendor, began rolling his thin Persian zulabias into cone shapes for ice cream vendor Arnold Fornachou who had run out of dishes. Multiple vendors at the fair claimed the invention, but the 1904 World's Fair is definitively credited with launching the cone's mass adoption.

The diesel engine was invented by Rudolf Diesel in Germany, who published his theoretical analysis in 1892 and demonstrated the first working engine in 1897. Diesel designed it to be more efficient than the steam engine and theorized that vegetable oils could be used as fuel — at the 1900 Paris Exhibition, his engine ran on peanut oil. The diesel engine now powers over 90% of the world's cargo ships.

The Band-Aid's design proved so successful that by 1924 Johnson & Johnson had moved to machine-made bandages and introduced a sterilization process. However, the first Band-Aids made in 1920 were entirely handmade, 18 inches long, and required the user to cut their own strips. The small individually wrapped bandage in its modern form only became available in 1926 after several years of refinement.

The helicopter in a practical form was first flown by Igor Sikorsky in his VS-300 on September 14, 1939 in Stratford, Connecticut. Earlier helicopter designs by Juan de la Cierva (autogyro, 1923) and Paul Cornu (1907) had achieved limited results. Sikorsky's single main rotor with tail rotor design became the dominant helicopter configuration used in over 90% of helicopters worldwide today.

Supermarket self-checkout was patented by Howard Schneider in 1992 and first installed at Price Chopper in Albany, New York, in 1994. While originally designed to reduce labor costs and speed checkout, self-checkout has been criticized for increasing theft and creating poor user experiences — a technology that succeeded commercially while generating ongoing debate about whether it is actually an improvement.

Lithium-ion batteries were developed by John Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino, who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Whittingham laid the foundations in the 1970s, Goodenough improved the cathode material in the 1980s (at age 57 — his most important work came after most scientists retire), and Yoshino created the first safe commercial cell in 1985.

Synthetic quinine — the antimalarial drug — was first synthesized in 1944 by Robert Woodward and William Doering at Harvard, a landmark achievement of total synthesis. While natural quinine from cinchona bark had been available since the 1600s, wartime shortages drove the synthesis effort, and the research established organic chemistry techniques still used in pharmaceutical development.

The safety razor was invented by King Camp Gillette in 1901, who patented a disposable double-edge blade that could be safely used without a barber's skill. Before safety razors, men either visited barbers or used dangerous straight razors; Gillette's disposable blade model — give away the handle, profit from the blades — became one of the most influential business models in consumer product history.

The cardboard milk carton was invented by John Van Wormer in 1915, who patented the 'Pure-Pak' wax-coated paperboard container after reportedly dropping a glass milk bottle and getting an idea. The container took decades to achieve widespread commercial adoption — the dairy industry resisted until the 1950s when waxing technology improved enough to prevent leaks consistently.

Radar-absorbing stealth materials were developed classified for decades before the F-117 Nighthawk first flew publicly in 1988. The mathematical foundation for low-observable radar-cross-section aircraft was published openly by Soviet physicist Pyotr Ufimtsev in 1964 — American Lockheed engineers used his equations to design the F-117 because Soviet authorities considered the paper too theoretical to be militarily useful.

The Pill was not the first hormonal contraceptive — Margaret Sanger and Katherine McCormick funded research by Gregory Pincus beginning in 1953, but Pincus relied on work by Carl Djerassi who had synthesized norethindrone in Mexico City in 1951 using a wild Mexican yam (Dioscorea mexicana) as the starting material for the first time a steroid was synthesized from a plant.

The pneumatic mail delivery system — tubes carrying canisters propelled by compressed air through underground pipes — was built in New York City in 1897 and by 1914 connected 22 post offices across 43 km of pipe, processing 30% of the city's mail. The system was abandoned in 1953 but inspired similar pneumatic systems still used to deliver documents in hospitals, banks, and airports.

Radar cross-section reduction through shape — the key principle of stealth aircraft design — was understood theoretically long before being applied practically. The unique faceted shape of the F-117 was required because 1970s computers could only calculate the radar reflection of flat surfaces; by the 1990s, curved stealth shapes (like the B-2 bomber) were feasible as computing power increased.

Surgical staples were invented in Hungary in the early 20th century by Hümér Hültl, who created a massive 8 kg machine in 1908 that stapled and cut tissue simultaneously. Modern surgical staplers are disposable single-use instruments that deploy rows of staples in milliseconds, joining bowel or blood vessels in seconds — a procedure that would take 20–30 minutes by hand suturing.

The first ATM (automated teller machine) was installed at Barclays Bank in Enfield, London, on June 27, 1967, dispensing cash in exchange for one-time use coded plastic tokens. Scottish inventor John Shepherd-Barron came up with the idea while in a bath, having arrived too late at his bank on a Saturday. The reusable plastic card and PIN combination he invented became the global standard for cash access.

The vending machine was invented in ancient Alexandria by Hero of Alexandria around 50 CE — it dispensed a fixed amount of holy water when a coin was dropped in and its weight activated a lever. The modern coin-operated vending machine for postcards and paper was patented in England in 1883 by Percival Everitt; Thomas Adams installed the first US gum machines at New York City elevated train platforms in 1888.

The digital camera image sensor — the CCD (charge-coupled device) — was invented by Willard Boyle and George Smith at Bell Labs in 1969, earning them the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics. The CCD converts photons to electrons and reads out the electrical signal to create an image; it is the foundational technology for digital cameras, smartphone cameras, astronomical telescopes, and medical endoscopes.

The Apgar score — a simple 10-point neonatal assessment invented by Virginia Apgar in 1952 — evaluates a newborn's Color, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration one and five minutes after birth. Apgar was the first woman to become a full professor at Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons; her score reduced neonatal mortality by enabling quick identification of infants needing immediate care.

The modern suspension bridge was pioneered by John Roebling, a German-American engineer who invented the twisted wire rope in 1841. His Brooklyn Bridge, opened in 1883, used wire rope cables he made himself and was the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time. Roebling died of tetanus after his foot was crushed during the bridge's initial survey; his son Washington completed the project.

Rayon — the first man-made textile fiber — was developed by French chemist Hilaire de Chardonnet in the 1880s by extruding cellulose nitrate through fine nozzles. Marketed as 'artificial silk,' it was flammable and expensive initially. Industrial viscose rayon, developed in England by Charles Cross and Edward Bevan in 1894, made cheap artificial silk widely available and disrupted the silk industry.

The DNA sequencing method — Sanger sequencing — was invented by Frederick Sanger at Cambridge in 1977, earning him his second Nobel Prize in Chemistry (his first was for determining the structure of insulin in 1958). Sanger sequencing remains in use today; the Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, used an automated version of Sanger sequencing to read all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA.

The escalator has become one of the most reliable and ubiquitous transportation inventions — yet it was nearly shelved when the original Reno design was shown at Harrods department store in London in 1898. An attendant was stationed at the top to offer smelling salts and cognac to ladies who found the experience too shocking. The device nonetheless caught on and Harrods still operates many of the longest escalators in the UK.

The Frisbee was invented by Fred Morrison in 1938 and evolved from the tradition of tossing pie tins from the Frisbie Pie Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut. Morrison sold his 'Pluto Platter' design to Wham-O in 1957 for $1 million in royalties over time; Wham-O renamed it 'Frisbee' — a deliberate misspelling of the pie company — and over 200 million have been sold, more than any other toy in history.

The parachute was independently conceived before Garnerin by Leonardo da Vinci, who sketched a pyramidal cloth parachute in 1485 with the caption 'If a man has a tent made of linen of which the apertures have all been stopped up... he will be able to throw himself down from any great height without sustaining any injury.' In 2000, parachutist Adrian Nicholas successfully jumped from 3,000 meters using a replica of da Vinci's design.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, the technique behind MRI, was developed as an analytical chemistry tool by Felix Bloch and Edward Purcell, who shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics. NMR became the chemist's most powerful tool for determining molecular structure, and the transition of NMR from chemistry laboratory to hospital radiology suite took 30 years and the insights of Lauterbur and Mansfield.

Tupperware was invented by Earl Tupper in 1946 using polyethylene plastic, but it flopped in stores. The invention only succeeded after Brownie Wise, a single mother from Michigan, developed the Tupperware Party model in 1948 — a direct sales system through home parties hosted by women. Tupper fired Wise in 1958 after she appeared on the cover of Business Week, becoming the first woman so honored, and she received no severance or stock.

The mechanical watch spring — the mainspring — was invented in Europe around 1400–1450, enabling watches small enough to be portable. The tourbillon — a rotating cage that counteracts the effect of gravity on balance wheel accuracy — was invented by Abraham-Louis Breguet in 1801. Modern mechanical watches, though less accurate than quartz, represent 600 years of continuous refinement of one of human history's most complex miniaturized mechanisms.

The HEPA (High Efficiency Particulate Air) filter was developed by the US Army Chemical Corps in the 1940s to capture radioactive particles. After declassification, it was commercialized for industrial use and eventually for home vacuum cleaners and air purifiers. A true HEPA filter must capture at least 99.97% of particles at 0.3 micrometers — including most bacteria, mold spores, and fine dust.

The first mechanical adding machine was invented by Blaise Pascal in 1642 at age 18 — motivated to ease his father's tax calculations. His Pascaline used a gear-based carry mechanism to add numbers automatically. Pascal built approximately 50 Pascalines but could not sell them commercially because they cost more to maintain than it would cost to hire a human calculator.

The Germ Theory of Disease — the revolutionary idea that infectious diseases are caused by microorganisms — was developed and proven by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch in the 1860s–1880s. Koch's postulates (1884) formalized how to prove a specific microbe causes a disease, and his methods are the basis of all subsequent bacteriology. Together, Pasteur and Koch's work enabled vaccines, antibiotics, and modern surgery.

The Otis safety elevator's impact on architecture was transformative — before it, no building was practical above five or six floors because few people would climb higher. After its commercial adoption in the 1870s, buildings could rise to any height, enabling the skyscraper boom of Chicago and New York in the 1880s–1890s and fundamentally changing how cities are designed and how dense they can become.

Chlorine as a water disinfectant was first applied in Jersey City, New Jersey in 1908, when the Boonton Reservoir supply was treated. Before routine water chlorination, waterborne diseases like typhoid killed tens of thousands in US cities annually; by the 1930s, widespread chlorination had reduced typhoid deaths in the US by over 90%. The CDC lists water chlorination as one of the top 10 public health achievements of the 20th century.

The remote control was invented by Nikola Tesla in 1898, when he demonstrated a radio-controlled boat at Madison Square Garden — he called it a 'teleautomaton.' He tried to sell the idea to the US Navy as an autonomous torpedo but was turned down. The TV remote control, invented by Robert Adler at Zenith in 1955, used ultrasound waves — the first versions had no batteries because Adler disliked cords.

The spreadsheet program — invented by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston as VisiCalc in 1979 — is credited with driving the first wave of personal computer adoption in business. VisiCalc did for numbers what a word processor did for text, and accountants and business owners bought Apple IIs specifically to run it. Some historians argue VisiCalc justified the entire personal computer industry and that without it, the PC revolution would have been delayed by years.

Paper currency was invented in China during the Tang Dynasty (618–907 CE) as 'flying money' (fei-qian) — merchants deposited coins with government offices and received paper certificates they could redeem elsewhere. By the Song Dynasty (960–1279 CE), the government issued official paper notes (jiaozi). Paper currency did not appear in Europe until the 17th century, developed independently by Swedish banks.

Bifocal lenses were invented by Benjamin Franklin around 1784 to avoid having to switch between reading glasses and distance glasses. Franklin cut two lenses in half and combined the halves, creating the first spectacles with two distinct focal lengths in a single frame. Franklin never patented his invention, and no contemporary documentation proves he invented bifocals — the attribution rests on letters he wrote describing using 'double spectacles.'
