The aerosol spray can was invented in 1941 by Lyle Goodhue and William Sullivan at the US Department of Agriculture to dispense insecticide against malaria-carrying mosquitoes in World War II. The 'bug bomb' — a heavy metal can with a valve — was developed into the consumer spray can by Robert Abplanalp in 1953, who invented the precision crimping technique that made leak-free lightweight aluminum cans possible.

The pencil was invented in England in 1565 when a large deposit of pure graphite was discovered at Borrowdale in Cumberland — the only large deposit of solid graphite ever found. Initially, graphite sticks were wrapped in string or sheepskin; the wooden casing was added around 1662. The pencil's name comes from the Latin 'penicillus' (little tail), reflecting its resemblance to a fine brush.

Touchscreen technology was first developed by E.A. Johnson at the Royal Radar Establishment in Malvern, England in 1965, for air traffic control displays. Resistive touchscreens were commercialized in the 1980s, but the capacitive multi-touch sensing that powers modern smartphones was developed at the University of Delaware in the 1970s and refined by Wayne Westerman, whose company was acquired by Apple in 2005.

The first electric iron was invented by Henry Seeley of New York in 1882, just three years after Edison demonstrated the first electric lighting system. Early electric irons had no thermostatic control and frequently burned clothing; the automatic thermostat was added by Joseph Myers in 1926. Before electricity, irons were heated on stoves and required constant swapping of heated and cooled units.

The bionic eye — a retinal prosthesis that partially restores vision to people blinded by retinal degeneration — received FDA approval as the Argus II in 2013. Developed by Second Sight Medical Products, it uses a camera on glasses to send signals to an electrode array implanted on the retina. The device provides sufficient vision to detect light, motion, and large shapes — not enough to read but enough to navigate independently.

The seatbelt as a three-point harness was invented by Nils Bohlin, a Volvo engineer, in 1959 — improving on two-point lap belts by crossing the body diagonally to hold both the pelvis and torso. Volvo made the three-point belt design freely available to all car manufacturers without charge, estimating that the invention has saved over a million lives since its introduction.

The first true aircraft, the Wright Flyer, flew for 12 seconds covering 37 meters on December 17, 1903 at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Wilbur and Orville Wright succeeded where well-funded competitors like Samuel Langley had failed largely because they developed a systematic approach to understanding aerodynamics — building their own wind tunnel to test wing shapes rather than relying on published (flawed) data.

Antiseptic surgery was pioneered by Joseph Lister in Glasgow in 1865, who applied Pasteur's germ theory to surgical infection. Using carbolic acid (phenol) spray to sterilize instruments, wounds, and the operating environment, he reduced post-surgical mortality from about 50% to under 15%. Listerine mouthwash, introduced in 1879, was named in his honor when it was marketed as a surgical antiseptic.

The submarine was first used militarily in the American Civil War — the Confederate H.L. Hunley in February 1864 became the first submarine to sink an enemy warship when it attacked the USS Housatonic. The Hunley then sank itself, killing its crew — the cause remains debated — and the wreck was recovered in 2000, now displayed at a preservation laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina.

The ATM PIN was originally proposed as a 6-digit number by inventor John Shepherd-Barron, but his wife Barbara said she could only remember four digits — so he shortened it to four. The 4-digit PIN has been the global standard ever since, though banks in some countries use 5 or 6 digits. Most PIN security depends not on length but on preventing repeated attempts through account lockout.

Polyethylene — the world's most widely produced plastic — was first accidentally created by Hans von Pechmann in 1898, but his discovery was unreproducible and forgotten. It was independently synthesized by accident again at ICI in England in 1933 by Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson when they pressurized ethylene and found a white waxy solid. Today over 100 million tonnes of polyethylene are produced annually.

The first commercial electric car predates the gasoline car — William Morrison built a 6-passenger electric carriage in Des Moines, Iowa in 1890, and by 1900 electric vehicles outsold gasoline cars in the United States. The internal combustion engine's lower cost, greater range, and faster refueling drove electrics from the market by the 1920s; a century later, electric vehicles are again outcompeting gasoline cars in many markets.

The printing press's most important innovation was not the press itself but Gutenberg's oil-based ink, which adhered to metal type and transferred sharply to paper — previous water-based inks simply beaded off metal. Gutenberg likely spent years perfecting the ink formula before his press was commercially viable, and the specific composition of his ink remained a trade secret during his lifetime.

The taser (a brand of conducted energy weapon) was invented by Jack Cover, a NASA scientist, in 1969 — the name is an acronym for 'Thomas A. Swift Electric Rifle,' a tribute to the Tom Swift adventure novel series Cover read as a child. Cover sold the device to a company founded by brothers Rick and Tom Smith in 1993; Taser International went on to deploy the device in most major US police departments.

Margarine was initially so disruptive to the dairy industry that Wisconsin banned it from 1895 until 1967 — a 72-year prohibition that made Wisconsin the last state in the US to legalize yellow margarine. Restaurants in Wisconsin were legally required to serve butter, and residents smuggled margarine from neighboring states. The law is a case study in how incumbent industries use regulation to suppress competing inventions.

The first synthetic antibiotic, prontosil, was discovered in 1932 by Gerhard Domagk at Bayer AG, who found that an azo dye cured bacterial infections in mice. He treated his own dying daughter with it successfully. Domagk won the 1939 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine but was forced to decline it by the Nazi government; he accepted the medal (but not the money) after the war.

The modern pencil eraser attached to the pencil end was invented independently in the USA by Hymen Lipman, who patented the combination in 1858. Joseph Reckendorfer bought the patent for $100,000 and sued Faber (pencil maker) for infringement; the US Supreme Court ruled in 1875 that combining two existing inventions (pencil + eraser) did not constitute a patentable invention — a landmark ruling on combinatorial innovation.

Insulin administration was revolutionized by the insulin pen — a cartridge-based injection device resembling a fountain pen — invented by Danish patient Sven Sorensen and introduced by Novo Nordisk in 1985. The pen injector replaced the vial-and-syringe method that required glass syringes boiled for sterilization; today over 90% of insulin-dependent diabetics in developed countries use pen injectors.

The modern shipping container was invented by American trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean in 1956, who created a standardized reusable steel box that could be transferred between truck, train, and ship without unpacking. Containerization reduced freight costs by 90%, enabling truly global supply chains — and it has been called the invention that made globalization possible.

The fiberscope — a flexible bundle of optical fibers for looking inside the body — was invented by Harold Hopkins and Narinder Singh Kapany in England in 1954, and converted for medical use by Basil Hirschowitz at the University of Michigan in 1957. Modern fiber optic endoscopes allow surgeons to operate inside joints, abdomens, and blood vessels through keyhole incisions, transforming surgery from open operations to minimally invasive procedures.

The push-button telephone replaced the rotary dial in the 1960s — Bell Labs introduced Touch-Tone service in 1963 using DTMF (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency) signaling, where each button produces two simultaneous tones. The system was resisted by many customers who preferred the tactile satisfaction of the rotary dial; by the 1980s, touch-tone phones had almost entirely replaced rotary dials in the USA.

The discovery that DNA is the molecule of heredity was made in 1944 by Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty at the Rockefeller Institute. Their 'transforming principle' experiment showed that purified DNA — not protein, as most scientists assumed — could transform bacteria. Avery was never awarded the Nobel Prize for this discovery, widely considered one of the greatest oversights in Nobel history.

The first food irradiation patent was issued to Charles Prescott and Samuel Sedgwick at MIT in 1905, after they demonstrated that X-rays could kill bacteria in food. The FDA approved food irradiation for spices in 1983 and poultry in 1990; despite being safe and effective, irradiated food remains unpopular with consumers who associate irradiation with radioactivity — though the process leaves no radioactive residue.

The photographic negative — which allows multiple positive prints from a single image — was invented by William Henry Fox Talbot in England in 1839, the same year Daguerre announced the daguerreotype in France. While the daguerreotype produced a superior single image, Talbot's negative-positive calotype process was more practical — the modern basis of film photography for 150 years.

The Concorde supersonic passenger aircraft was jointly developed by British and French aerospace manufacturers and entered commercial service in 1976. It cruised at Mach 2.04 (2,179 km/h) and crossed the Atlantic in under 3.5 hours. The Concorde program never broke even financially — the aircraft could not fly supersonic over land due to sonic boom regulations, limiting it to transatlantic routes — and the aircraft was retired in 2003.

The synthetic blood substitute — hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers and perfluorocarbon emulsions that can temporarily replace blood's oxygen-carrying function — have been developed since the 1980s but none has yet achieved widespread clinical adoption. The challenge is replicating the complex biology of red blood cells; current 'artificial blood' products are used only in emergency situations when compatible donor blood is unavailable.

The concept of the patent as a social contract — inventors disclose how something works in exchange for a temporary monopoly — was established in the Statute of Monopolies (1624) and later enshrined in the US Constitution (Article I, Section 8). Thomas Jefferson, as the first US Patent Examiner, personally reviewed and approved the first 67 patents — arguing strenuously that trivial inventions should not receive protection.

The food can's pull-ring tab was so successful it caused an environmental crisis in the 1970s — discarded rings littered beaches, highways, and parks, cutting human and animal feet. In 1975, Daniel Cudzik at Reynolds Metals patented the Stay-On tab (SOT), in which the ring stays attached to the can when opened. By 1980, virtually all US beverage cans used the SOT design, eliminating the litter problem.

The neonatal incubator was developed in the 1880s by French obstetrician Stéphane Tarnier, who visited a zoo and noticed chicken eggs being warmed in incubators. He commissioned a similar device for premature infants at the Paris Maternité hospital; mortality of premature infants at the hospital fell from 66% to 38% within two years. Martin Couney later popularized incubators by exhibiting premature babies in them at world's fairs.

The mechanical metronome was invented by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel in Amsterdam in 1814 and commercialized (with theft of the invention) by Johann Nepomuk Maelzel in 1815 — Beethoven was among the first composers to use Maelzel's metronome markings in his scores. The double-pendulum principle Winkel discovered enables the constant-period beating that Maelzel patented without crediting the inventor.

Chloroprene rubber (Neoprene) was invented by DuPont chemist Arnold Collins in 1930 when he accidentally produced a new rubbery material while working with vinylacetylene. Neoprene was the first synthetic rubber to achieve commercial success, valued for its resistance to oil, heat, and weathering that natural rubber lacks — essential for wetsuits, automotive hoses, and electrical insulation.

The word processor was created not by Silicon Valley but by IBM in 1964, with the MT/ST (Magnetic Tape Selectric Typewriter), which allowed text to be stored on magnetic tape and reprinted without retyping. WordStar for microcomputers (1978) and later WordPerfect and Microsoft Word brought word processing to desktop computers and transformed every office, newsroom, and university in the world.

Solar water heating was first commercialized by Baltimore inventor Clarence Kemp in 1891 with his 'Climax' solar water heater — a black tank inside a glass-covered box. By 1941, 60,000 homes in Florida had solar water heaters, but cheap natural gas and electricity after World War II killed the market. Solar water heating has recently revived as the most efficient solar technology available, with China now installing more capacity than the rest of the world combined.

The automatic bread slicer was invented by Otto Frederick Rohwedder in 1928 and first used at the Chillicothe Baking Company in Missouri on July 7, 1928. Rohwedder worked on the invention for 16 years — a fire destroyed his first prototype in 1917 — and faced years of skepticism that sliced bread would go stale too quickly. The expression 'the best thing since sliced bread' dates to its wildly enthusiastic reception.

Cochlear implants were initially opposed by many in the Deaf community, who viewed deafness as a cultural identity rather than a disability to be 'fixed.' The debate intensified in the 1990s as parents chose implantation for children too young to consent, raising profound ethical questions about medical intervention, cultural identity, and what counts as disability — questions that continue alongside advancing bionic technology.

The ballistic missile was first developed as the V-2 by Wernher von Braun and his team at Peenemünde for Nazi Germany, with the first successful test on October 3, 1942. At an altitude of 84.5 km, the V-2 became the first man-made object to reach space. After the war, von Braun and key team members were recruited by the USA under Operation Paperclip to develop the rockets that eventually carried Americans to the Moon.

The Analytical Engine designed by Charles Babbage between 1833 and 1871 was a proposed mechanical general-purpose computer a century before electronic computers. It was never completed in his lifetime, but Ada Lovelace, Countess of Lovelace, wrote extensive notes on the machine including what is recognized as the first computer algorithm — and she predicted in 1843 that the engine could be used to compose music.

The most consequential single invention in human history is disputed — candidates include writing (~3200 BCE, Mesopotamia), the wheel (~3500 BCE), the printing press (1440 CE), the steam engine (1712), germ theory/vaccines (1796), and the internet (1969–1991). Each transformed civilization, but writing arguably encompasses all others: it is the technology that allows inventions to be recorded, shared, and built upon, making all subsequent invention possible.

The barometer was invented in 1643 by Italian physicist Evangelista Torricelli, a student of Galileo, who filled a glass tube with mercury and inverted it into a dish — the column of mercury dropped to about 76 cm, proving that atmospheric pressure, not a vacuum, holds up fluids.

The safety pin was invented in 1849 by American mechanic Walter Hunt, who created it in just three hours to pay off a $15 debt; he sold the patent rights immediately for $400 and never profited further from what became one of the most ubiquitous fasteners in the world.

The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by French physician René Laennec, who rolled sheets of paper into a cylinder to listen to a patient's heart — the paper tube amplified sounds far better than placing his ear directly on the chest, and he later refined the design using wood.

The revolver was patented in 1836 by Samuel Colt at age 21, featuring a rotating cylinder that held multiple rounds and could be fired in sequence without reloading after each shot; the Colt Patterson was the first commercially produced revolver and transformed both warfare and frontier life in America.

text: The sewing machine was patented in 1846 by Elias Howe with a lockstitch mechanism, but it was Isaac Singer who made it commercially successful in 1851 by adding a foot pedal and a straight needle; Singer also pioneered the installment payment plan to make the machines affordable to working-class families.

The saxophone was invented around 1840 by Belgian instrument maker Adolphe Sax, who combined the reed mouthpiece of a woodwind with the conical metal body of a brass instrument; he patented it in 1846, and it was initially used in military bands before becoming central to jazz.

The hypodermic needle was independently developed around 1853 by Scottish physician Alexander Wood and French surgeon Charles Pravaz; Wood used it to inject morphine directly into tissue for pain relief, and his wife reportedly became the first recorded person to die from a hypodermic drug overdose.

Dynamite was invented in 1867 by Alfred Nobel, who stabilized the notoriously volatile nitroglycerin by absorbing it into diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr); Nobel was motivated partly by the death of his younger brother Emil in a nitroglycerin explosion, and he later used his fortune from dynamite patents to fund the Nobel Prizes.

The typewriter was commercially introduced by Remington & Sons in 1874 based on the design of Christopher Latham Sholes; the QWERTY keyboard layout Sholes devised was specifically arranged to reduce jamming of mechanical keys by placing frequently paired letters apart from each other.

The internal combustion engine was first developed practically by Belgian engineer Étienne Lenoir in 1859, using a mixture of coal gas and air ignited by an electric spark; Karl Benz later refined the four-stroke gasoline engine in 1885 and built the first true automobile powered by it.

The zipper was invented by Whitcomb Judson in 1893 as a 'clasp locker' for shoes, but it was Swedish-American engineer Gideon Sundback who perfected the modern interlocking-teeth design in 1913; the name 'zipper' was coined by the B.F. Goodrich Company when it used the fastener on rubber galoshes in 1923.

Aspirin was first synthesized in a stable form by Felix Hoffmann at Bayer in 1897; the active ingredient, acetylsalicylic acid, had been known since the 1850s, but Hoffmann's synthesis made it safe enough for mass production, and Bayer began selling it as a powder in 1899.

The paperclip was patented by Norwegian inventor Johan Vaaler in 1899, though a similar design had been in use in Britain for some years prior; during World War II the paperclip became a symbol of Norwegian national resistance against the Nazi occupation, with citizens wearing them to show solidarity.

The vacuum cleaner was invented by Hubert Cecil Booth in 1901, who got the idea by watching a railway car cleaner blow dust around and reasoning that sucking would be more effective; his first machine was so large it had to be pulled by a horse-drawn carriage and operated from outside buildings through long hoses.

The air conditioner was invented in 1902 by Willis Carrier, a 25-year-old engineer hired to solve a humidity problem at a Brooklyn printing plant; his system used chilled coils to remove moisture from the air, and the first residential air conditioners became available in the 1920s.

The windshield wiper was invented in 1903 by Mary Anderson, who noticed during a New York City streetcar ride that the driver had to stop and clear the windshield manually in the rain; her patent for a swinging arm with a rubber blade was initially dismissed by manufacturers as a distraction to drivers.

The sonar system was first developed during World War I by French physicist Paul Langevin and Russian engineer Constantin Chilowsky in 1917 to detect German submarines; it used piezoelectric quartz to generate and detect ultrasonic waves, and the acronym SONAR (Sound Navigation And Ranging) was coined in the 1940s.

Cellophane was invented in 1908 by Swiss chemist Jacques Brandenberger, who was trying to create a stain-proof tablecloth; when he coated a fabric with viscose, the film peeled off as a transparent sheet, leading him to develop it as a standalone packaging material that transformed the food industry.

The crossword puzzle was invented by journalist Arthur Wynne and first published in the New York World newspaper on December 21, 1913; it was diamond-shaped with no black squares, and the simple word game evolved into a global phenomenon with dedicated publications and championship competitions.

The pop-up toaster was invented by Charles Strite in 1919, a factory worker in Stillwater, Minnesota, who was tired of the burnt toast served in the company cafeteria; he designed a spring mechanism and timer to automatically eject toast when done, receiving a patent in 1921.

Insulin was isolated and purified by Canadian researchers Frederick Banting and Charles Best in 1921 at the University of Toronto; the first diabetic patient treated, 14-year-old Leonard Thompson, nearly died from a crude first injection but was successfully treated with a purified version on January 23, 1922.

The adhesive bandage (Band-Aid) was invented in 1920 by Earle Dickson, a Johnson & Johnson employee, to help his accident-prone wife Josephine; he pre-made strips of tape with gauze attached and showed them to his employer, who began marketing them commercially in 1924.

Sliced bread was first sold commercially on July 7, 1928, by the Chillicothe Baking Company in Missouri, using a bread-slicing machine invented by Otto Rohwedder; the phrase 'the greatest thing since sliced bread' entered common use within a few years of this invention.

The jet engine was independently invented by Frank Whittle in Britain (patent 1930) and Hans von Ohain in Germany (patent 1936); the German He 178 aircraft made the world's first jet-powered flight on August 27, 1939, just days before the start of World War II.

The electron microscope was invented in 1931 by German physicists Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll, achieving magnifications far beyond what light microscopes could reach; Ruska received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986 — 55 years after his invention — one of the longest gaps between invention and recognition in Nobel history.

The parking meter was invented by Carlton Magee and first installed in Oklahoma City on July 16, 1935; inspired by a coin-operated newspaper box, it was designed to combat downtown congestion caused by office workers who parked all day, leaving no spots for customers.

Nylon was invented by Wallace Carothers at DuPont in 1935 and first used commercially in nylon-bristle toothbrushes in 1938; when nylon stockings went on sale in the US on May 15, 1940, four million pairs sold in the first day, demonstrating the enormous pent-up demand for synthetic silk alternatives.

The photocopier (Xerox machine) was invented by Chester Carlson in 1938 using a process he called electrophotography, later renamed xerography; despite demonstrating the technology in 1939, Carlson was rejected by over 20 companies including IBM and General Electric before the Haloid Company (later renamed Xerox) agreed to develop it.

Velcro was invented in 1941 by Swiss engineer George de Mestral, who noticed that burdock burrs clung to his dog's fur after a walk; examining them under a microscope, he saw tiny hooks that caught on loops, and after years of development he patented the two-sided fastener in 1955.

The microwave oven was invented accidentally in 1945 by Percy Spencer, a Raytheon engineer working with radar magnetrons, who noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted; he then intentionally tested the heating effect and developed the first commercial microwave oven, the 'Radarange,' in 1947.

The credit card was introduced by Diners Club in 1950, created by Frank McNamara after he reportedly forgot his wallet at a restaurant; the original cardboard card was accepted at 27 New York City restaurants and had 200 cardholders, growing to 20,000 within the first year.

The bar code was invented in 1952 by Norman Woodland and Bernard Silver, who drew on their knowledge of Morse code to create a pattern of dots and dashes that could be scanned optically; the first product scanned using a barcode at retail checkout was a pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum on June 26, 1974.

The nuclear submarine was pioneered by US Navy Captain Hyman Rickover, and USS Nautilus (SSN-571) was launched in 1954 as the world's first nuclear-powered vessel; in 1958 Nautilus became the first submarine to travel beneath the geographic North Pole, navigating 1,830 miles under Arctic ice.

source.name: US Navy Naval History and Heritage Command

text: The hard disk drive was invented by IBM engineer Reynold Johnson and introduced in 1956 with the IBM 350 Disk File; it had 50 magnetic disks each 24 inches in diameter, weighed over a ton, and stored 5 MB of data — a capacity now exceeded by a single digital photo.

The laser was first demonstrated by Theodore Maiman on May 16, 1960, using a synthetic ruby rod and a photography flash lamp; the acronym LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, a concept theorized by Albert Einstein in 1917.

The liquid-crystal display (LCD) was invented in 1964 by George Heilmeier at RCA's research laboratories in New Jersey; Heilmeier demonstrated a working LCD device and showed it could display numbers, though the technology would not reach commercial prominence until the 1970s in calculators and watches.

The computer mouse was invented by Douglas Engelbart at the Stanford Research Institute in 1964 and was first demonstrated publicly on December 9, 1968 — in what became known as 'The Mother of All Demos' — alongside videoconferencing, collaborative editing, and hypertext, all decades before they became mainstream.

The ATM (Automated Teller Machine) was first installed by Barclays Bank in Enfield, London, on June 27, 1967; actor Reg Varney was the first customer to withdraw cash, and the machine used single-use paper vouchers pre-ordered from the bank as early PIN-equivalents, as magnetic stripes were not yet in use.

The smoke detector was patented in 1969 by Duane Pearsons and a team at BRK Electronics, building on ionization technology developed by Swiss physicist Walter Jaeger in the 1930s; when battery-powered home units became widely available in the 1970s, residential fire deaths in the US fell dramatically over the following decades.

The floppy disk was invented by IBM engineer Alan Shugart and introduced commercially in 1971; the original 8-inch disks stored 80 KB of data, and subsequent generations shrank to 5.25 inches and then 3.5 inches while increasing capacity — a progression that continued until USB flash drives made floppy disks obsolete in the early 2000s.

The CT scanner (computed tomography) was invented by Godfrey Hounsfield of EMI Laboratories in England and independently by Allan Cormack; the first clinical CT scan was performed in 1972 on a patient with a suspected brain tumor, and Hounsfield and Cormack shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1979.

The Post-it Note was invented accidentally at 3M by Spencer Silver in 1968, who created a weak pressure-sensitive adhesive but couldn't find a use for it; colleague Art Fry later used it to keep bookmarks in his hymnal in 1974, and the product finally launched commercially in 1980 after initial test markets showed strong demand.

The MRI scanner (magnetic resonance imaging) was developed by Raymond Damadian, who demonstrated the first whole-body MRI scan in 1977; Peter Mansfield and Paul Lauterbur won the 2003 Nobel Prize for their work on MRI, controversially excluding Damadian, who took out full-page newspaper ads protesting the omission.

The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by Hungarian professor Ernő Rubik as a teaching tool to help students understand three-dimensional geometry; it took Rubik himself over a month to solve the puzzle he created, and after licensing to Ideal Toy Corp, it became the best-selling puzzle game in history with over 350 million sold.

The Walkman was introduced by Sony on July 1, 1979, revolutionizing how people listened to music by making it personal and portable; Sony co-founder Masaru Ibuka requested a portable stereo cassette player so he could listen to opera on long flights, and the device transformed youth culture worldwide in the 1980s.

The Teflon coating was invented accidentally by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938 when a canister of tetrafluoroethylene gas failed to discharge during an experiment; the white waxy residue turned out to be polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), one of the most slippery substances known, and was first used commercially in the Manhattan Project before appearing on cookware in the 1960s.

The World Wide Web was invented by British scientist Tim Berners-Lee while working at CERN in 1989; he wrote his original proposal in March 1989, and his supervisor famously wrote 'Vague but exciting' on it — the first website went live on December 20, 1990, and Berners-Lee chose not to patent his invention, making it freely available to all.

The lithium-ion battery was developed by John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham, and Akira Yoshino in the 1970s–80s, winning the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019; at 97, Goodenough became the oldest Nobel laureate in any discipline and continued researching improved solid-state batteries well into his late 90s.

The GPS (Global Positioning System) was developed by the US Department of Defense and became fully operational on April 27, 1995, with 24 satellites in orbit; it was originally exclusively for military use, but President Reagan ordered it made available for civilian use after Korean Air Lines Flight 007 was shot down in 1983 due to a navigation error.

The USB (Universal Serial Bus) standard was developed by a group of seven companies led by Ajay Bhatt of Intel and introduced in 1996 to replace the confusing tangle of serial, parallel, and other ports on PCs; Bhatt's invention is so fundamental that Intel used him in a celebrity-style commercial campaign, making him one of the few chip engineers to achieve popular recognition.

Kevlar was invented by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont in 1965, who discovered a liquid crystalline polymer solution that produced fibers five times stronger than steel by weight; initially dismissing what seemed like a faulty batch, she insisted on testing the unusual solution, leading to a material now used in bulletproof vests, tires, and spacecraft.

The pacemaker was first successfully implanted by Swedish surgeon Åke Senning in 1958, using a device built by engineer Rune Elmqvist; the first recipient, Arne Larsson, outlived both his surgeon and the inventor of the device, dying in 2001 at age 86 after receiving 26 pacemakers throughout his lifetime.

The compact disc (CD) was jointly developed by Sony and Philips and launched in Japan in October 1982; the disc diameter of 12 cm was reportedly chosen so it could hold all 74 minutes of Beethoven's 9th Symphony as performed by Herbert von Karajan — though this romantic story has been disputed by some engineers involved.

The Super Soaker water gun was invented by NASA engineer Lonnie Johnson in 1989; Johnson was working on an environmentally friendly heat pump using water instead of freon when he accidentally shot a powerful stream of water across his bathroom, inspiring the toy that has sold over 200 million units and made him one of the most successful Black inventors in US history.

The artificial heart was first successfully implanted in a human by Dr. Denton Cooley in 1969 as a temporary bridge to transplant; the first permanent total artificial heart, the Jarvik-7, was implanted in Barney Clark in 1982 by Dr. William DeVries — Clark survived 112 days connected to a refrigerator-sized air compressor.

The digital camera was invented by Kodak engineer Steven Sasson in 1975; the first prototype weighed 8 pounds, captured black-and-white images at a resolution of 0.01 megapixels onto a cassette tape, and took 23 seconds to record a single image — Kodak shelved the invention fearing it would cannibalize film sales.

The World Wide Web search engine was pioneered by the Archie tool (1990), but the modern search engine concept emerged with WebCrawler (1994) and AltaVista (1995); Google was founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin as a Stanford PhD project, built on the PageRank algorithm that evaluated a page's importance by counting inbound links.

The airbag was invented by John Hetrick, an industrial engineer, who patented it in 1953 after a near accident with his family; independently patented by German inventor Walter Linderer the same year, airbags were not installed in production cars until the 1970s and only became federally mandated in US vehicles in 1998.

The spray can (aerosol) was patented by Norwegian engineer Erik Rotheim in 1927, but it was American chemist Lyle Goodhue who developed the practical insecticide aerosol 'bug bomb' in 1941 to protect US soldiers from malaria-carrying mosquitoes in the Pacific; the technology was later adapted for hairspray, deodorant, and paint.

The microprocessor was invented by Intel engineers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, and Stanley Mazor, resulting in the Intel 4004, released on November 15, 1971; this first microprocessor had the same computing power as the ENIAC computer of 1945 but fit on a chip the size of a fingernail, beginning the era of personal computing.

The escalator was patented by Jesse Reno in 1892, and the first practical 'inclined elevator' was installed as a novelty ride at Coney Island in 1896; Otis Elevator Company acquired the competing Seeberger design, coined the name 'escalator,' and installed the first department store escalator at the Philadelphia store of Gimbels in 1901.

The mechanical clock with a verge escapement was developed in medieval Europe around 1275–1300 CE, replacing water clocks and sundials; these early clocks had no minute or second hands and were accurate only to within 15 minutes per day, but they fundamentally reorganized European society around measured, mechanical time.

Concrete was used extensively by the Romans, who created opus caementicium using volcanic ash (pozzolana), lime, and seawater; Roman marine concrete structures have lasted over 2,000 years, and modern researchers discovered in 2023 that the seawater reaction actually strengthens the concrete over time — the opposite of modern Portland cement.

The safety match was invented in 1844 by Swedish chemistry professor Gustaf Erik Pasch, who separated the reactive components so that the match could only ignite when struck on a specially prepared surface; this replaced 'strike-anywhere' matches that could ignite accidentally and caused numerous fires.

The phonograph was invented by Thomas Edison in 1877; he shouted 'Mary had a little lamb' into the device's mouthpiece, and when he played it back and heard his own voice for the first time, he was reportedly so surprised he could hardly believe his ears — it was the first device capable of recording and reproducing sound.

The modern bicycle with a chain drive and equal-sized wheels (the 'Safety Bicycle') was invented by John Kemp Starley in 1885, replacing the dangerous penny-farthing; it triggered a massive cycling craze and, crucially, gave women unprecedented freedom of independent movement — Susan B. Anthony called it 'the freedom machine.'

The Haber-Bosch process for synthesizing ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen was developed by Fritz Haber (1909) and scaled industrially by Carl Bosch; it enabled mass production of nitrogen fertilizers and is credited with allowing Earth's population to grow from 1.6 billion in 1900 to over 8 billion today — roughly half of all nitrogen atoms in the human body come from synthetic fertilizer.

The thermos (vacuum flask) was invented by Scottish chemist James Dewar in 1892, who used a double-walled glass vessel with a vacuum between the walls to minimize heat transfer; Dewar never patented it, and German glassblower Reinhold Burger commercially produced it as the 'Thermos' — a name chosen by public competition in 1904.

The electric iron was invented in 1882 by Henry W. Seely of New York City, who patented an iron connected via cord to an electrical outlet; early models were dangerous as they had no thermostat, and the first thermostatic electric iron was not introduced until 1927 by Eldec Corporation, making the appliance significantly safer.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The contact lens was first conceptualized by Leonardo da Vinci in 1508 and prototyped by René Descartes in 1636, but the first glass contact lenses were ground and fitted by German ophthalmologist Adolf Eugen Fick in 1888; modern soft contact lenses made from hydrogel were invented by Czech chemist Otto Wichterle in 1961.

The combine harvester was invented by Hiram Moore and John Hascall in 1834 and first used on a large scale in California's wheat fields in the 1880s; a single modern combine can harvest up to 250 acres per day and has reduced the agricultural workforce so dramatically that less than 2% of Americans now work in farming compared to over 90% in colonial times.

The refrigerator was first patented in 1834 by Jacob Perkins using a vapor-compression cycle with ether; the first practical household electric refrigerator, the Domelre (domestic electric refrigerator), was introduced in Chicago in 1913, and by 1944 over 85% of American families owned one — one of the fastest adoptions of any appliance in history.

The CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool was developed by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier in 2012, adapting a bacterial immune defense mechanism into a precise tool to cut and edit DNA; they were awarded the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and the technology has since been used to treat sickle cell disease in humans.

The electric light bulb was developed by Thomas Edison in 1879 using a carbonized bamboo filament that lasted over 1,200 hours; however, English inventor Joseph Swan had developed a working incandescent bulb months earlier, and after a patent dispute both men formed a joint company — Edison & Swan United Electric Light Company — in 1883.

The assembly line was pioneered by Henry Ford at his Highland Park plant in 1913 for the Model T, reducing the time to build a car from over 12 hours to 93 minutes; Ford also doubled workers' wages to $5 per day — not purely out of generosity, but because high turnover in the new factory system was costing more than the wage increase.

The can opener was invented 48 years after the tin can itself; Ezra Warner patented the first can opener in 1858, with the tin can having been invented by Peter Durand in 1810 — during those 48 years, cans were opened with hammers and chisels, and early army rations included instructions to use a bayonet.

The contraceptive pill was developed by Gregory Pincus and John Rock, with crucial financial support from feminist activist Margaret Sanger and heiress Katharine McCormick; the FDA approved Enovid as a contraceptive on May 9, 1960, and within two years, 1.2 million American women were using it, fundamentally reshaping reproductive autonomy.

The touchscreen was invented by E.A. Johnson at the Royal Radar Establishment in England around 1965 and published in a 1967 paper; capacitive touchscreens were developed by Frank Beck and Bent Stumpe at CERN in the early 1970s, and multi-touch technology was refined at Bell Labs and University of Toronto before being popularized by the iPhone in 2007.

Cement production dates to ancient Rome, but Portland cement was invented by English bricklayer Joseph Aspdin in 1824, who named it after Portland stone because of its similar color; his son William later improved the formulation by using higher kiln temperatures, producing the cement that forms the basis of all modern concrete construction.

The fire sprinkler system was invented by Henry Parmalee in 1874 to protect his piano factory in New Haven, Connecticut; the modern fusible-link sprinkler that activates individually (so only sprinklers near the fire discharge) was patented by Frederick Grinnell in 1881, and this remains the fundamental design used in buildings worldwide today.

Vulcanized rubber was invented by Charles Goodyear in 1839 through an accidental discovery — he dropped a mixture of rubber and sulfur onto a hot stove and found the result was elastic, stable, and heat-resistant; despite receiving a patent in 1844, Goodyear died in debt in 1860 after spending his fortune on failed ventures.

The telegraph was invented by Samuel Morse (USA) and Charles Wheatstone (England) independently in the 1830s; Morse's system with its dot-dash code transmitted the famous first long-distance message 'What hath God wrought?' from Washington D.C. to Baltimore on May 24, 1844, using a line built along the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The gyroscope was invented by French physicist Léon Foucault in 1852, who used it to demonstrate Earth's rotation; the spinning device maintains its orientation in space regardless of surrounding movement and is now central to navigation systems in ships, aircraft, smartphones, and spacecraft.

The modern zipper-style hearing aid was preceded by ear trumpets used since the 17th century, but the first electric hearing aid was created by Miller Reese Hutchison in 1898; the first wearable, transistor-based hearing aid was introduced by Sonotone Corporation in 1952, reducing the device from tabletop size to something that fit behind the ear.

The eraser was attached to a pencil for the first time by Hymen Lipman, who received US Patent 19,783 in 1858; in 1875, the US Supreme Court invalidated the patent, ruling it was merely a combination of two existing inventions, not a new one — establishing an important legal precedent that combining existing inventions doesn't always merit a patent.

The electric guitar was invented by George Beauchamp and Adolph Rickenbacker around 1931, creating what they called the 'Frying Pan' lapsteel guitar; the solid-body electric guitar was commercialized by Leo Fender's Telecaster (1950) and Gibson's Les Paul (1952), fundamentally transforming popular music.

The 3D printer was invented by Chuck Hull in 1984, who developed stereolithography (SLA), using ultraviolet lasers to cure photopolymer resin layer by layer; Hull co-founded 3D Systems Corporation and holds over 60 patents related to 3D printing, which today is used in aerospace, medicine, and consumer goods manufacturing.

The pedal-powered bicycle pump was preceded by Robert Boyle's first air pump (1659), which he used to prove that sound cannot travel through a vacuum by placing a bell inside and evacuating the air; this experiment was foundational to understanding that sound requires a medium, a fact now taught in every physics class.

The modern traffic light was invented by Garrett Morgan, a Black inventor from Cleveland, who installed the first three-position traffic signal (go, stop, and an intermediate 'all-stop' position) at the intersection of 105th Street and Euclid Avenue in Cleveland in 1923; he later sold the patent to General Electric for $40,000.

The first working prototype of television was demonstrated by John Logie Baird on January 26, 1926, at the Royal Institution in London using a mechanical scanning system; Baird used a ventriloquist's dummy named 'Stooky Bill' as his subject because its high-contrast painted face transmitted better than human skin under early studio lighting.

The transistor was invented on December 23, 1947, by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs; the three shared the Nobel Prize in 1956, but Shockley later founded Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory, whose employees left to start Fairchild Semiconductor, whose alumni then founded Intel — a genealogy that birthed Silicon Valley.

The supermarket was invented by entrepreneur Michael J. Cullen, who opened 'King Kullen' in Jamaica, Queens, New York on August 4, 1930; it was the first store to offer customers self-service shopping across a wide variety of products at low prices, replacing the clerk-assisted model of traditional grocery stores.

The modern surgical anesthesia was pioneered on October 16, 1846, when dentist William Morton publicly demonstrated ether anesthesia at Massachusetts General Hospital in a procedure now called 'Ether Day'; the discovery that surgery could be performed painlessly transformed medicine, and the operating theater where it occurred is preserved as the 'Ether Dome.'

The jacquard loom was invented by Joseph Marie Jacquard in Lyon, France in 1804, using punched cards to automate complex fabric patterns; Charles Babbage was directly inspired by Jacquard's punched-card system when designing his Analytical Engine, and it later influenced Herman Hollerith's punched-card tabulating machine used in the 1890 US Census.

The bulletproof vest was first developed in the 1880s using layers of silk; Dr. George Goodfellow documented that several Tombstone gunfight victims were stopped by folded silk handkerchiefs, and Casimir Zeglen developed a wearable silk vest in 1897 that could stop low-velocity bullets fired from close range.

The photovoltaic solar cell was invented by Bell Labs scientists Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, and Gerald Pearson in 1954, achieving 6% efficiency; the first commercial use was on the Vanguard I satellite in 1958, and modern solar cells now exceed 47% efficiency in laboratory conditions, though typical commercial panels achieve 20–22%.

The automated teller machine (ATM) PIN was invented by Scottish engineer John Shepherd-Barron, who originally wanted a six-digit number but his wife Caroline said she could only remember four; her preference established the global four-digit PIN standard that now secures billions of bank accounts worldwide.

The parachute was first demonstrated by André-Jacques Garnerin on October 22, 1797, jumping from a hydrogen balloon at 3,200 feet over Paris in a frameless silk canopy; the lack of a vent hole caused violent oscillations, and the vent was later added by astronomer Jérôme Lalande — the same design principle still used in modern parachutes.

The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique was invented by Kary Mullis in 1983, who conceived the idea while driving along Highway 128 in California; the method for amplifying DNA sequences won him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993 and became foundational to genetic testing, forensics, and COVID-19 diagnostics.

The standardized shipping container was invented by trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean, who loaded the first containerized cargo ship, the Ideal X, in Newark, New Jersey on April 26, 1956; economist Marc Levinson estimated that containerization reduced shipping costs by 97%, enabling modern globalization and transforming the world economy.

The mechanical calculator was invented by Blaise Pascal in 1642 at age 18, to help his father with tax calculations; he called it the 'Pascaline,' and while he built around 50 machines, they were too expensive to manufacture and maintain, meaning clerks remained cheaper than the machines for another two centuries.

The piano was invented around 1700 by Italian harpsichord maker Bartolomeo Cristofori, who called it 'gravicembalo col piano e forte' (harpsichord with soft and loud); unlike the harpsichord, the piano's hammer mechanism allowed players to control volume by touch, making it one of the most expressive instruments ever built.

The first synthetic dye, mauveine (mauve), was discovered accidentally in 1856 by 18-year-old British chemistry student William Henry Perkin while attempting to synthesize quinine; his discovery launched the synthetic dye industry, made purple affordable to the masses (previously only royalty could afford it), and founded modern organic chemistry.

The diving suit was first patented by Augustus Siebe in 1837, creating the 'closed' helmet suit that allowed divers to breathe supplied air and work at depth; Siebe's design was used to salvage the wreck of the Royal George in the 1840s, and his basic principle — a sealed suit with externally supplied air — remained standard for over a century.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The tin can was patented by Peter Durand in England in 1810 under a commission from the British Royal Navy, who needed a way to preserve food for soldiers and sailors during the Napoleonic Wars; the cans were made of thick iron tinned with a thin layer of tin, and they were so thick that a label was required stating 'cut around the top near the outer edge with a chisel and hammer.'

The snowboard was invented by Sherman Poppen in 1965 as a Christmas gift for his daughter; he attached two skis together and added a rope to hold while surfing down hills, calling it the 'Snurfer'; inspired by skateboarding and surfing, it evolved through the work of Jake Burton Carpenter and Tom Sims into the modern snowboard, which became an Olympic sport in 1998.

The first commercially successful helicopter was the Sikorsky R-4, developed by Igor Sikorsky and produced from 1942; Sikorsky had fled Russia after the Bolshevik Revolution, rebuilt his aviation career in the US, and his single-rotor design with a tail rotor for torque compensation became the standard helicopter configuration used worldwide.

The vending machine dates to ancient Alexandria, where Hero of Alexandria designed a machine around 50 CE that dispensed holy water when a coin was inserted into a slot and pressed a lever; the first modern coin-operated vending machines were installed in London in the 1880s, dispensing postcards and books.

The cotton gin was invented by Eli Whitney in 1793 in just ten days while visiting a Georgia plantation; by mechanizing the separation of cotton fiber from seeds, it increased production 50-fold, but its unintended consequence was making cotton farming so profitable that the demand for enslaved labor surged, significantly expanding and entrenching American slavery.

The first steam-powered locomotive was built by Richard Trevithick in Wales and made its inaugural run on February 21, 1804, hauling 10 tons of iron and 70 passengers over 9.75 miles; the heavy weight broke the cast-iron rails, and practical railway transportation awaited George Stephenson's improved locomotives on stronger wrought-iron tracks.

Bifocal eyeglasses were invented by Benjamin Franklin around 1784, who was frustrated by needing to switch between two pairs of glasses for reading and distance; he cut two lenses in half and combined them in a single frame, and though he mentioned them in letters, he never patented the invention.

The Bessemer process for mass-producing steel was patented by Henry Bessemer in 1855, allowing cheap steel to replace expensive wrought iron; the process worked by blowing air through molten pig iron to burn off impurities, reducing the cost of steel by about 80% and enabling the great age of steel bridges, railways, and skyscrapers.

The dishwasher was invented by Josephine Cochrane in 1886; after servants kept chipping her fine china while washing it, she designed a machine using water pressure to spray jets of hot soapy water, patented the design, and exhibited it at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where hotels and restaurants immediately placed orders.

The first successful gasoline-powered automobile was built by Karl Benz in Mannheim, Germany, and patented on January 29, 1886; in 1888, his wife Bertha took their two teenage sons on the world's first long-distance automobile journey — 66 miles from Mannheim to Pforzheim — without telling Karl, stopping at a pharmacy for fuel and inventing brake pads along the way.

The disposable razor was invented by King Camp Gillette in 1903, who was inspired by bottle cap inventor William Painter to create a product that would be thrown away after use, ensuring repeat purchases; the first year's sales were only 51 razors and 168 blades, but by 1904 it sold 90,844 razors and 123,648 blades.

Celluloid, the first synthetic plastic, was invented by John Wesley Hyatt in 1869 in response to a $10,000 prize offered by a billiard ball manufacturer for an alternative to ivory; while celluloid proved unsuitable for billiard balls (it was too flammable), it transformed photography, film, and later the dental and film industries.

The linotype machine was invented by German-American watchmaker Ottmar Mergenthaler in 1886 and first used by the New York Tribune; by casting entire lines of type at once instead of one letter at a time, it revolutionized newspaper publishing and dominated typesetting until phototypesetting replaced it in the 1970s.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The modern stapler was patented by Henry R. Heyl in 1877, and the first stapler designed to hold a cartridge of staples was patented by E.H. Hotchkiss in 1895; the Swingline stapler, iconic in office culture, was introduced in 1925 and popularized loading staples from the top, which became the standard design.

The modern flush toilet is often misattributed to Thomas Crapper; it was actually invented by Alexander Cumming in 1775, who patented the S-bend pipe that prevents sewer gases from entering the building — the most important feature of the modern toilet. Thomas Crapper was a real plumber who popularized flush toilets in England but did not invent them.

The frozen food industry was created by Clarence Birdseye, who invented a quick-freezing process in 1924 after observing Inuit people in Labrador, Canada, quick-freeze freshly caught fish in the Arctic winter; he noticed the rapid freezing preserved flavor far better than slow freezing, and sold his patents and company to Postum (later General Foods) in 1929 for $22 million.

The jukebox was invented in San Francisco on November 23, 1889, when Louis Glass and William Arnold installed a coin-operated Edison phonograph at the Palais Royale Saloon; for a nickel, customers could select one of four listening tubes — it was an immediate success, earning $1,000 in less than six months.

The photoelectric cell was first described by Heinrich Hertz in 1887, when he noticed that ultraviolet light caused metal electrodes to spark more easily; Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect in his famous 1905 paper (for which he won the 1921 Nobel Prize), and this understanding became the basis for solar cells, light meters, and digital cameras.

The aerosol hairspray was introduced by Chase Products Company in 1948 using Freon as the propellant; the invention of CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons) as propellants by Thomas Midgley Jr. in 1928 initially seemed like a breakthrough, but the widespread use of CFCs in aerosols later contributed to the depletion of the ozone layer, leading to the Montreal Protocol of 1987.

The hovercraft was invented by British engineer Christopher Cockerell in 1956, who tested the concept using a cat food can inside a coffee tin with a hairdryer; his SR.N1 crossed the English Channel on July 25, 1959 — the 50th anniversary of Blériot's first crossing by airplane — and hovercraft passenger services ran until 2000.

The aqua-lung (SCUBA) was co-invented in 1943 by French naval officer Jacques Cousteau and engineer Émile Gagnan, who adapted a car gas regulator to control the flow of compressed air; their invention liberated divers from cumbersome surface-supplied air hoses, opening the ocean for exploration and spawning a global sport diving industry.

The Polaroid instant camera was invented by Edwin Land in 1948, inspired by his three-year-old daughter who asked why she couldn't see a photo immediately after it was taken; Land had the idea and completed the theoretical design within an hour, and the Polaroid Land Camera 95 sold out its first production run on its first day at Jordan Marsh department store in Boston.

The Segway was invented by Dean Kamen and launched with massive hype in December 2001 after entrepreneur John Doerr predicted it would be 'bigger than the internet'; despite its innovative self-balancing gyroscope technology, it never became a mass transportation device and was primarily used by police forces, tourists, and warehouse workers.

The ballpoint pen was invented by Hungarian journalist László Bíró in 1938, who was frustrated that fountain pen ink smeared and took too long to dry; he adapted printer's ink (which dried quickly) with a rotating ball bearing tip, and the British Royal Air Force ordered 30,000 'Biros' in 1944 because they worked at high altitudes where fountain pens leaked.

The first programmable computer, the Z3, was built by German engineer Konrad Zuse in 1941 using telephone relays in his parents' living room in Berlin; Zuse's work was largely isolated from Allied developments due to WWII, and he is often overlooked in computing history despite predating the better-known ENIAC (1945) by four years.

The Fahrenheit scale was invented by German physicist Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit in 1724; he set 0°F as the lowest temperature he could achieve in his lab (a brine solution), 32°F as the freezing point of water, and 96°F as human body temperature (later corrected to 98.6°F), producing a scale that remains in use only in the United States and a few other countries.

The first mass-produced plastic, Bakelite, was invented by Belgian-American chemist Leo Baekeland in 1907; it was the first truly synthetic plastic — not derived from any natural material — and its heat-resistant, non-conductive properties made it ideal for early electronics, from radio cabinets to telephone handsets.

The ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer), the first general-purpose electronic computer, was completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania; it was programmed primarily by six women — Frances Bilas Spence, Jean Jennings Bartik, Kathleen McNulty Mauchly Antonelli, Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, and Betty Holberton — whose contributions went largely unrecognized for decades.

source.name: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing

text: The escalator was originally trademarked rather than patented — Otis Elevator Company registered 'escalator' as a trademark in 1900, and it remained a protected brand name until 1950 when a court ruled it had become a generic term for all moving stairways; this 'genericide' of trademarks (also affecting Band-Aid, Thermos, and Zipper) is a significant concern for brand owners.

The modern fire extinguisher was patented by British captain George Manby in 1818, using a copper vessel containing potassium carbonate solution expelled by compressed air; a more familiar form using soda-acid was patented by Almon Chubb in 1881, and today's dry chemical extinguishers trace back to improvements made in Germany in the 1940s.

The washing machine was first patented in America by Nathaniel Briggs in 1797 as a hand-cranked wooden box with a wringer; the first electric washing machine was introduced by Hurley Machine Corporation in 1908 under the brand name Thor, and by 1940 over 60% of US homes with electricity had an electric washing machine.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The seed drill was invented by Jethro Tull in England around 1701, allowing seeds to be planted in straight rows at a controlled depth and spacing rather than scattered by hand; Tull's invention dramatically improved crop yields and seed efficiency and laid foundations for scientific agriculture, though it was initially resisted by farm laborers who feared it would take their jobs.

The catapult was first developed in ancient Greece around 400 BCE; Greek historian Diodorus described its invention at Gela in Sicily, and the Romans later refined it into the 'onager' and 'ballista' designs capable of hurling 300-pound stones over 300 yards — a range not significantly exceeded until the development of artillery in the 14th century.

The integrated circuit was simultaneously and independently invented by Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments in 1958 and Robert Noyce of Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959; Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work (Noyce had died in 1990), and the integrated circuit enabled miniaturization that made smartphones, laptops, and modern electronics possible.

The first true programmable digital computer using vacuum tubes was the Colossus, built at Bletchley Park in Britain in 1943 to break the German Lorenz cipher; classified for 30 years after the war, its existence and the genius of its creator Tommy Flowers were kept secret, preventing him from receiving credit he deserved during his lifetime.

The modern bicycle chain was invented by Hans Renold in Manchester, England in 1879 using a bush roller chain design; Renold's chain was so superior to existing drive mechanisms that it became the standard for bicycles, motorcycles, and eventually automobiles, and the Renold chain design remains fundamentally unchanged in bicycles today.

Cellphone technology traces back to the first cellular call made by Martin Cooper of Motorola on April 3, 1973, using a prototype DynaTAC phone; Cooper called rival Joel Engel at Bell Labs from a street corner in Manhattan, and the first commercial cellular network was not available to the public until 1983 — a decade after that inaugural call.

Chewing gum was patented as a commercial product by Thomas Adams in 1871, who had originally worked with Mexican General Antonio López de Santa Anna to try to use chicle (tree sap) as a rubber substitute; when that failed, Adams boiled the chicle and chewed it, recognized its potential, and began manufacturing flavored chicle gum.

The periscope was invented independently by several people but the submarine periscope was patented by Thom Subi in 1854 and later improved by John Phillip Holland; during World War I, German U-boats used periscopes to locate and sink Allied ships while remaining hidden, and improvements in anti-periscope aircraft spotting became a critical element of anti-submarine warfare.

The pocket watch was invented in Nuremberg, Germany around 1510 by clockmaker Peter Henlein, who created a portable spring-driven clock small enough to be carried on the person; early models only had an hour hand, and it was not until the late 1700s that accurate enough movements allowed minute and second hands to be added.

The thermometer was invented by Galileo Galilei around 1593 as a rudimentary 'thermoscope' that showed temperature changes but had no scale; Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit created the first mercury thermometer with a reliable scale in 1714, and Anders Celsius developed his 100-degree scale in 1742, originally with 0° as the boiling point and 100° as freezing.

Braille was developed by Louis Braille, who lost his sight at age three in a workshop accident and entered the Paris school for the blind; at age 15 in 1824, he adapted a military communication system called 'night writing' into a six-dot cell system that he published at age 20 — it was not officially adopted by France until 1854, two years after his death.

The spinning jenny was invented by English weaver James Hargreaves in 1764, reportedly after he accidentally knocked over his wife Jenny's spinning wheel and noticed it continued to spin while vertical; the machine allowed one worker to spin eight threads simultaneously (later 80), dramatically reducing the cost of cotton thread and sparking the textile revolution.

The concrete pump was invented in Germany in 1927 by Fritz Hull, allowing liquid concrete to be moved through pipes directly to where it was needed; this invention transformed high-rise construction by eliminating the need to manually carry or crane concrete to upper floors, enabling the rapid skyscraper building booms of the 20th century.

The shopping cart was invented by Sylvan Goldman, owner of the Piggly Wiggly and Humpty Dumpty supermarket chains in Oklahoma, in 1937; noticing customers stopped shopping when their hand baskets became too heavy, he mounted wire baskets on a folding chair with wheels — but shoppers initially refused to use them, so he had to hire people to push them around as models.

The modern ski binding was developed by Norwegian Sondre Norheim in the 1860s, who created a fixed heel binding from twisted birch root that allowed for much greater control and enabled skiing to evolve from a purely practical transportation method into a sport; Norheim is considered the 'father of modern skiing' and designed the first modern ski jump.

The Frisbee traces its origins to Yale students in the 1920s tossing the empty pie tins from the Frisbie Baking Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut; Walter Frederick Morrison designed a plastic flying disc in 1948 and sold the design to Wham-O in 1957, which renamed it the 'Frisbee' (a deliberate misspelling to avoid trademark issues with the pie company).

The safety elevator with a fail-safe mechanism was invented by Elisha Otis in 1852; he demonstrated his 'safety elevator' dramatically in 1854 at the Crystal Palace Exposition in New York by riding the platform up and then having an assistant cut the rope — the braking mechanism held, and the stunned audience realized tall buildings were now viable.

The Lego brick was invented by Danish carpenter and toy maker Ole Kirk Christiansen in 1932, and the iconic interlocking plastic brick design was patented in 1958; the name comes from the Danish 'leg godt' meaning 'play well,' and Lego manufactures over 36 billion bricks annually — enough to circle the Earth more than five times placed end to end.

The modern lifejacket (personal flotation device) was invented in Norway in 1854 by Captain Ward; early versions were simply cork blocks sewn into canvas vests, and the design evolved slowly until WWII, when the 'Mae West' inflatable vest was developed, named by Allied pilots because the inflated chest section resembled the famous actress's figure.

The Thermos (vacuum flask) trademark became so popular that a 1963 US court decision ruled it had become genericized — meaning any manufacturer could call their vacuum flask a thermos; this made Thermos one of the most famous examples of 'genericization,' where a brand becomes synonymous with the product category.

The phonograph needle (stylus) evolved from Edison's steel needle to a diamond stylus; the diamond stylus, first introduced commercially in the 1940s, is virtually indestructible and can play tens of thousands of records without wearing out, whereas steel needles needed replacement after every few plays and accelerated groove wear.

The modern flush toilet's S-bend was invented by Alexander Cumming in 1775; before the S-bend, even 'water closets' smelled because there was nothing to prevent sewer gases from rising through the drain. Cumming's innovation of the water-filled S-shaped trap below the bowl is still the standard in every flush toilet manufactured today.

Smokeless powder (nitrocellulose-based) was invented by French chemist Paul Vieille in 1884, replacing black powder in firearms; it produced far less smoke, was more powerful, and did not foul the barrel as quickly — enabling the semi-automatic and automatic weapons of the 20th century and making black powder firearms obsolete virtually overnight.

The lock and key was invented in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia around 4,000 years ago, using large wooden pin-tumbler locks; the metal pin-tumbler lock was reinvented by Linus Yale Jr. in 1861, and his design — a small flat key with serrated edges that lifts a series of spring-loaded pins — is the standard used in virtually all residential door locks today.

The Yo-Yo is one of humanity's oldest toys, with evidence dating back to ancient Greece around 500 BCE; the name comes from the Filipino language and the toy was used as a hunting weapon in the Philippines, though this is now disputed; Pedro Flores, a Filipino immigrant, started the first Yo-Yo manufacturing company in the US in 1928.

The solar water heater was first patented by Clarence Kemp of Baltimore in 1891; his 'Climax' solar heater was a black-painted tank mounted in a glass-covered box on the roof that heated water for domestic use without any fuel cost, and by 1897, 30% of homes in Pasadena, California, were using solar water heaters.

The percolator coffee maker was invented by American soldier Benjamin Thompson (Count Rumford) around 1810, though the pump percolator was patented by Illinois farmer Hanson Goodrich in 1889; the drip coffee maker was introduced by German housewife Melitta Bentz in 1908, who placed a piece of blotting paper in a brass pot to filter out bitter grounds.

The food processor was invented by French catering equipment salesman Pierre Verdun, who introduced the 'Robot Coupe' machine at a Paris trade show in 1971; American inventor Carl Sontheimer licensed the technology, refined it for home kitchen use, and launched the Cuisinart in the US in 1973, transforming home cooking.

The wristwatch was developed from a pocket watch fitted to a bracelet in the 1880s, and while Patek Philippe made a wristwatch for Hungarian Countess Koscowicz in 1868, the first mass-market wristwatch for men was made by Girard-Perregaux for German Kaiser Wilhelm's navy in 1880; wristwatches were still considered feminine novelties until WWI soldiers found them essential for coordinating attacks.

The lawn mower was invented in 1830 by English textile engineer Edwin Budding, who got the idea from a nap-cutting machine used to trim the pile on velvet cloth; before its invention, lawns at large estates were kept by teams of scythe workers, making manicured lawns a symbol of wealth that the mower eventually democratized.

The hydrometer, used to measure liquid density, was invented by Hypatia of Alexandria around 400 CE, making her one of the first women inventors recorded in history; Hypatia was also a mathematician and philosopher who ran a school in Alexandria before being murdered by a Christian mob in 415 CE.

The folding umbrella was invented in China around the 11th century CE and the European umbrella as a rain protector dates to 1750s London, popularized by Jonas Hanway who openly carried an umbrella for 30 years despite ridicule; hackney carriage drivers initially opposed umbrellas because dry people preferred to hire cabs, and they reportedly attacked Hanway.

The programmable thermostat was invented by Warren Johnson, who also founded Johnson Controls in 1883; Johnson was a professor who was frustrated by having to ask janitors to adjust building temperatures, so he invented a system of pneumatic tubes that allowed temperature to be controlled remotely, laying the groundwork for building automation.

The incubator for premature infants was developed by French obstetrician Stéphane Tarnier in 1880, inspired by a warming box he saw at the Paris Zoo used for chick eggs; before its introduction, premature infant survival rates were below 35%, but at the Maternité de Paris, survival rates rose to over 66% after the incubator was introduced.

The first self-propelled vehicle was built by French engineer Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot in 1769 for hauling artillery; the steam-powered three-wheeled vehicle could travel at about 4 km/h but had to stop every 10-15 minutes to build up steam pressure, and Cugnot is recorded as having the world's first automotive accident when he crashed it into a stone wall.

The neon sign was invented by French engineer Georges Claude, who demonstrated neon-filled glass tubes producing orange-red light at the Paris Motor Show in December 1910; he brought neon signs to the US in 1923, selling two signs to a Los Angeles Packard dealership for $1,250 each, and the glowing signs became so popular they were called 'liquid fire.'

The electric toothbrush was first invented by Dr. Philippe-Guy Woog in Switzerland in 1954 under the brand name Broxodent and was initially marketed to people with limited motor skills and orthodontic patients with braces; General Electric introduced a cordless rechargeable version for the mass market in the US in 1961.

The loom dates back to prehistoric times, but the power loom — driven by a water wheel or steam engine — was invented by Reverend Edmund Cartwright in 1784; despite having no engineering training, Cartwright's invention was so disruptive to hand-weavers that in 1812, a mob of weavers burned down a factory that had installed his looms.

The retractable ballpoint pen was invented by Hungarian-American László Bíró's brother György Bíró, an engineer who helped improve the original design; the retractable click mechanism for pens was later perfected by Waterman and Parker, but the most famous version, the Bic Cristal, was introduced in France in 1950 and is the world's best-selling pen with over 100 billion sold.

The lie detector (polygraph) was invented by John Augustus Larson, a University of California Berkeley student, in 1921, building on the systolic blood pressure test of William Moulton Marston; Marston, who also created Wonder Woman as a symbol of 'truth-telling,' was ironically not given credit for the foundational blood pressure test when Larson built on it.

Bubble wrap was invented in 1957 by engineers Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes, who were originally trying to create a textured wallpaper by sealing two shower curtains together with air pockets; after the wallpaper idea flopped, they pivoted to packaging material, and Sealed Air Corporation (which they co-founded) now sells over $4 billion worth of packaging products annually.

The Heimlich maneuver for choking victims was developed by Dr. Henry Heimlich in 1974 and published in the journal Emergency Medicine; by applying upward abdominal thrusts to expel a foreign object from the airway, the technique has reportedly saved tens of thousands of lives, including Dr. Heimlich himself using it at age 96 to save a fellow retirement home resident.

The pop tab on aluminum cans was invented by Ermal Fraze in 1959 after he was forced to use a car bumper to open a can of beer at a picnic; he developed the integral pull-tab that was attached to the lid, and the modern 'stay-tab' (which stays attached after opening) was invented by Daniel Cudzik at Reynolds Metals in 1975 to address litter problems.

The modern pencil with a graphite core was invented in 1565 after a large deposit of graphite was discovered in Borrowdale, England; the graphite (initially mistaken for a form of lead, hence 'lead pencil') was so pure that it could be sawed into rods and inserted into wooden casings, a technique still used today.

The Richter scale for measuring earthquake magnitude was developed by seismologists Charles Richter and Beno Gutenberg at Caltech in 1935; it was a logarithmic scale where each whole number increase represents a tenfold increase in measured amplitude and roughly 31.6 times more energy released, and it has largely been replaced by the moment magnitude scale since the 1970s.

The electronic synthesizer was pioneered by Robert Moog, who designed the first commercially sold modular synthesizer in 1964; the Moog synthesizer was popularized by Wendy Carlos's 1968 album 'Switched-On Bach,' proving that electronic instruments could produce music of serious classical quality and opening the door to the entire genre of electronic music.

The magnetic stripe card was invented by IBM engineer Forrest Parry in 1960, who was tasked with attaching a magnetic tape to a plastic ID card for the CIA; frustrated by his inability to bond the materials, he brought the card home, and his wife suggested using a clothes iron — and it worked, launching the technology now found on over 8 billion credit and debit cards.

The gas turbine engine for aircraft was invented by Hans von Ohain in Germany (patented 1936) and Frank Whittle in Britain (patented 1930) independently; the first jet aircraft powered by Whittle's engine design was the Gloster Meteor, which entered RAF service in 1944 and was used to intercept German V-1 flying bombs — the first jet-versus-jet engagements in history.

The Muzak company was founded in 1934 by General George Squier, who had invented a system of transmitting music through electrical power lines; 'background music' was initially designed to reduce anxiety in elevator riders (hence 'elevator music') and later used in factories to increase worker productivity — studies at the time claimed it increased output by 11%.

The Bunsen burner was invented in 1855 by German chemist Robert Bunsen in collaboration with laboratory mechanic Peter Desaga; despite being named for Bunsen, the primary designer was Desaga, who built on an earlier design by Michael Faraday — the burner remains one of the most fundamental pieces of chemistry equipment 170 years later.

The compact fluorescent lamp (CFL) was invented by Edward Hammer at General Electric in 1976 in response to the energy crisis, achieving 75% energy savings over incandescent bulbs; GE chose not to manufacture it due to the high tooling costs, and the design was reverse-engineered by Chinese manufacturers, eventually leading to CFLs becoming cheaper than incandescents.

The LED (light-emitting diode) was invented by Nick Holonyak Jr. at General Electric in 1962, producing visible red light; Shuji Nakamura invented the blue LED in 1994 (for which he won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics), enabling the white LEDs that now dominate lighting — blue was the missing color needed to combine RGB LEDs into white light.

The first practical computer spreadsheet, VisiCalc, was invented in 1979 by Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston; it was the 'killer app' that drove sales of the Apple II computer, and the concept of the recalculating spreadsheet — where changing one cell automatically updates all related cells — revolutionized business accounting and financial modeling.

The mechanical loom's punched card inspiration led to the development of the Hollerith punched card, used by Herman Hollerith to tabulate the 1890 US Census in one year — a process that would have taken eight years by hand; Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company in 1896, which later merged with others to form IBM in 1924.

The modern zipper fastener achieved widespread acceptance only after B.F. Goodrich used it in boots (1923) and when the fashion designer Elsa Schiaparelli featured zippers prominently in her 1930 collection; before that, buttons were so entrenched that early users had to be literally trained to use zippers, with manuals sometimes provided.
