The MRI's underlying phenomenon, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), was discovered simultaneously in 1946 by Felix Bloch at Stanford and Edward Purcell at Harvard, who shared the 1952 Nobel Prize in Physics; it took another 25 years before Raymond Damadian and Paul Lauterbur recognized that NMR could be used to image the human body.

The intermittent windshield wiper was invented by Robert Kearns in 1963, inspired by the way a human eye blinks; he patented his design and then watched Ford Motor Company introduce an identical system in 1969 without licensing his patent — he spent 30 years in legal battles and eventually won $30 million from Ford and $11.5 million from Chrysler.

The submarine telegraph cable connecting Britain to the US was laid aboard the SS Great Eastern in 1866 after two failed attempts; Cyrus West Field spent 12 years and several fortunes trying to connect the continents by wire, and the successful connection made it possible to exchange news between London and New York in minutes rather than weeks.

The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, was launched by the Soviet Union on October 4, 1957, and transmitted radio signals back to Earth for three weeks before its batteries died; its launch shocked the United States and directly led to the creation of NASA (1958), the space race, and eventually the first Moon landing in 1969.

The jackhammer (pneumatic drill) was invented by Samuel Ingersoll in 1871, building on the concept of using compressed air to drive a drill bit; its first major use was boring tunnels through the Mont Cenis pass in the Alps, and it later became ubiquitous in mining, quarrying, and road construction worldwide.

The seismograph was invented by Chinese polymath Zhang Heng in 132 CE, a device he called the 'earthquake weathervane' (houfeng didong yi); it featured a pendulum inside a bronze vessel surrounded by dragons — when an earthquake occurred, the pendulum swung and dropped a ball into the mouth of a frog, indicating the direction of the quake.

The modern safety bicycle tire (pneumatic rubber tire) was reinvented for bicycle use by Scottish veterinarian John Boyd Dunlop in 1887 for his son's tricycle — he wrapped rubber tubing around the wheels and inflated it with a soccer ball pump; Dunlop was unaware that Robert Thomson had patented a similar idea in 1845, which had been forgotten.

The Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (Harvard Mark I) was completed in 1944 through the collaboration of IBM and Howard Aiken at Harvard; it was 51 feet long, 8 feet tall, and weighed 5 tons, executing three additions per second — Admiral Grace Hopper programmed it and later coined the term 'bug' when her team found a literal moth jammed in its relays.

The disposable diaper was invented by Marion Donovan in 1946, a Yale-educated mother who first made a waterproof diaper cover from a shower curtain and then developed a fully disposable version; she was rejected by every major manufacturer, so she sold her covers herself at Saks Fifth Avenue, then sold the patent for $1 million — just as Procter & Gamble was preparing to launch Pampers.

The optical fiber was developed by Chinese-American physicist Charles Kao (who won the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics) and George Hockham at Standard Telecommunications Laboratories in 1966; Kao demonstrated that glass fibers could transmit light over long distances if impurities were removed, and today over 1 billion km of optical fiber spans the globe carrying the internet's data.

The hydraulic press was invented by Joseph Bramah in 1795, who applied Pascal's law to create a machine that used water pressure to generate enormous mechanical force; Bramah also invented the flush toilet cistern mechanism and the unpickable Bramah lock, and he offered £200 to anyone who could pick his lock — it remained unpicked for 67 years.

The automatic vending machine for postage stamps was installed by the British Post Office in 1867; by 1888 Thomas Adams installed automatic gum machines on New York City elevated train platforms, and the candy and cigarette vending machine industry exploded in the early 20th century, becoming a multibillion-dollar global business.

The liquid-fueled rocket was first successfully launched by Robert Goddard on March 16, 1926, in Auburn, Massachusetts; his 10-foot rocket flew 41 feet and reached an altitude of 12 meters in 2.5 seconds — a modest beginning, but it established the fundamental principles behind every rocket launch from the Saturn V to Falcon 9.

The fluoride toothpaste was developed through the research of Dr. Frederick McKay, who in 1909 noticed that residents of Colorado Springs, Colorado, had unusually low rates of tooth decay despite having brown-stained teeth; decades of research revealed it was caused by naturally occurring fluoride in the water, and fluoride toothpaste reached American consumers in 1960 with Crest.

The modern zipper's biggest rival was initially the button, which had been used since the Bronze Age; in fact, the earliest known buttons — made of curved shells — date to the Indus Valley Civilization around 2000 BCE and were used decoratively, not functionally, as buttonholes were not invented until around 1200 CE in Germany.

The first vaccine was created by Edward Jenner in 1796, who noticed that milkmaids who caught cowpox did not get smallpox; he inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with cowpox pus and then, controversially by modern standards, exposed him to smallpox — the boy did not develop the disease, and Jenner's vaccination (from 'vacca,' Latin for cow) launched immunology.

The rubber band was patented by Stephen Perry of London in 1845, made from vulcanized rubber developed by Charles Goodyear; Perry's company, Messers Perry and Co., mass-produced the bands which became indispensable in offices and homes worldwide — the Alliance Rubber Company is now the world's largest rubber band manufacturer, producing over 100 million pounds annually.

Chillwave pasta machinery was preceded by the food extruder, which was first developed in the US meat packing industry; the concept was applied to pasta manufacturing in Italy in the early 20th century, and the modern pasta extrusion machine, which forces dough through shaped dies under high pressure, enabled mass production and global export of Italian pasta shapes.

The pneumatic tube mail system was first proposed by William Murdoch in the early 19th century; the London Pneumatic Dispatch Company built a tunnel in 1863 to deliver mail by compressed air under the streets of London, and New York City operated a pneumatic mail system from 1897 to 1953 capable of delivering 100,000 letters per hour.

The contact microphone (pickup) for electric guitar was invented by Lloyd Loar at Gibson Guitar in the early 1920s; however, it was the magnetic pickup — invented by George Beauchamp and applied to the Rickenbacker 'Frying Pan' guitar in 1931 — that became the standard for amplifying guitar strings without feedback.

source.name: Smithsonian National Museum of American History

text: The retinal prosthesis (bionic eye) was first developed by Mark Humayun and colleagues at the University of Southern California; the Argus II system received FDA approval in 2013, using a camera on glasses that sends signals to electrodes implanted in the retina — the first commercially available device restoring partial sight to people blinded by degenerative retinal disease.

The Gatling gun was invented by Richard Gatling in 1861 and first used in battle during the American Civil War; Gatling, a physician, reportedly invented it because he hoped its devastating firepower would reduce the size of armies needed (and thus casualties), demonstrating a long history of weapons inventors rationalizing their creations as tools of peace.

The hearing aid as a device evolved from ear trumpets used since the 1600s to the carbon microphone hearing aid in 1898; the vacuum tube hearing aid (1920s) enabled electronic amplification, and the critical breakthrough was the transistor hearing aid introduced by Sonotone Corporation in 1953, shrinking the device from suitcase-size to behind-the-ear.

Polyester was invented by British chemists John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson in 1941 at the Calico Printers' Association; they built on Wallace Carothers' earlier work on polyamides (nylon) and created a fiber they called Terylene, which was later commercialized by ICI in Britain and DuPont as Dacron in the US.

The modern brassiere was patented in the US in 1914 by Mary Phelps Jacob (later Caresse Crosby), who fashioned it from two handkerchiefs and a pink ribbon on the night of a formal dinner when her corset showed through her sheer gown; she sold the patent to the Warner Brothers Corset Company for $1,500 — who went on to earn $15 million from it.

The can of condensed milk was invented by Gail Borden in 1856 and first made commercially viable with an industrial canning process; Borden developed it after witnessing children die of milk-borne disease on a transatlantic voyage and was motivated to create a safer preserved milk; the product became critically important for feeding Union soldiers during the Civil War.

The first successful powered airplane flight was by Orville Wright on December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, lasting just 12 seconds and covering 120 feet; the Wright Brothers achieved what others couldn't by focusing on control (wing warping) rather than power, and Orville's historic flight was witnessed by only five people including a local lifeguard.

The crash-test dummy was invented by Samuel Alderson in 1949 for use in aviation ejection seat tests; the automotive crash dummy, Sierra Sam, was developed in 1949, and General Motors introduced the first Hybrid II dummy in 1972, specifically designed to measure injuries to vehicle occupants and now used in regulatory testing worldwide.

The artificial sweetener saccharin was discovered accidentally in 1879 by Constantin Fahlberg, a chemist working at Johns Hopkins University who noticed his food tasted sweet after a day in the lab; he tasted his hand and traced the sweetness to a compound he had accidentally spilled — though he failed to wash his hands, leading to the discovery.

The plow dates to at least 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia as a simple 'scratch plow' (ard), but the heavy moldboard plow that could turn dense northern European soils was developed around the 6th century CE; this innovation dramatically increased agricultural output in Northern Europe and is credited by some historians with enabling the medieval population explosion.

Scotch tape (cellophane tape) was invented by Richard Drew at 3M in 1930, initially created to help auto body workers paint two-tone cars without the tape tearing apart; its transparent and waterproof properties made it a versatile general-purpose adhesive tape, and the iconic plastic dispenser with the serrated edge was introduced in 1932.

The defibrillator was invented by Claude Beck, a cardiac surgeon at Western Reserve University who performed the first successful defibrillation of a human heart in 1947 on a 14-year-old boy during open-heart surgery; the patient had no pulse, and Beck used internal paddles to shock the heart directly, restoring normal rhythm.

Play-Doh was invented in 1956 by Noah McVicker as a non-toxic wallpaper cleaning compound made from flour, water, salt, and boric acid; his sister-in-law, a nursery school teacher, started using it as a modeling clay for children, and McVicker reformulated and remarketed it as a toy — becoming one of the most popular children's toys in history with over 2 billion cans sold.

The electric motor was independently invented by Michael Faraday (1821, England) and Joseph Henry (1831, USA); Faraday's rotating wire in a magnetic field was the first electromagnetic rotation device, and his later discovery of electromagnetic induction in 1831 led to both the motor and the generator — Faraday called it 'the conversion of magnetism into electricity.'

The modern parachute with a ripcord was invented by Leo Stevens in 1908; prior to his innovation, parachutes were attached to the aircraft and deployed automatically when the jumper fell away, making intentional delayed jumps (and thus skydiving) impossible; the ripcord gave jumpers control over when to open their chute.

The coin-operated piano (nickelodeon) was invented by John Gabel in 1897 and became the first mass-market music playback device in public spaces; when the Wurlitzer company added record-playing technology in the 1930s to create the jukebox, it displaced the mechanical piano and transformed how Americans consumed popular music in diners, bars, and drive-ins.

The modern life straw (portable water filter) traces back to ancient times when cloth filters were used in India and Egypt; the modern LifeStraw product was designed in 2005 by Vestergaard Frandsen to filter waterborne pathogens in developing countries, capable of filtering up to 1,000 liters of contaminated water per device without electricity or replacement parts.

The cat flap was reportedly invented by Isaac Newton, who cut two holes in his door for his cat and her kittens; while there is no definitive historical documentation of this, Newton's colleague William Stukeley mentioned it, and the concept of a small hinged door for cats is documented in Cambridge from Newton's era.

The concept of the internet originated with ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), which sent its first message on October 29, 1969, between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute; the first message was 'login,' but the system crashed after 'lo' — making 'lo' the accidental first words of the internet age.

The piston steam engine was invented by Thomas Newcomen in 1712 to pump water out of Cornwall tin mines; though highly inefficient, it ran for decades until James Watt dramatically improved efficiency in 1769 by adding a separate condenser — Watt's improved engine was so fundamental to industrialization that the unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

The polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) branded as Teflon was accidentally discovered by Roy Plunkett at DuPont in 1938; it was classified as a military secret during WWII when used in uranium enrichment for the Manhattan Project, and it did not appear on cookware until French engineer Marc Grégoire invented a method to bond it to aluminum pans in 1954.

The rebreather for divers was invented by Henry Fleuss in 1878 using oxygen and potassium hydroxide to absorb carbon dioxide, allowing divers to breathe the same gas repeatedly without bubbles; it was first used to repair a flooded tunnel in 1880, and modern closed-circuit rebreathers allow divers to remain underwater for hours using a fraction of the gas an open-circuit SCUBA system requires.

The first commercially available personal computer was the Altair 8800, introduced on the cover of Popular Electronics magazine in January 1975; it had no keyboard, no monitor, and no software, but it inspired a young Bill Gates and Paul Allen to write a BASIC interpreter for it — they founded Microsoft in 1975 specifically for this product.

The synthetic rubber neoprene was invented by DuPont chemist Arnold Collins in 1930 while studying the polymerization of acetylene — he found a rubbery material accidentally left in a flask; neoprene resists oils, fuels, and weathering better than natural rubber, making it essential for wetsuits, gaskets, and cable insulation.

The submarine torpedo was invented by British engineer Robert Whitehead in 1866 working for the Austrian Navy; self-propelled and steerable, it used a compressed-air engine and gyroscope for directional control, and it revolutionized naval warfare, making the capital ship vulnerable to small torpedo boats for the first time in history.

The solar panels that power most satellites trace back to Vanguard I, launched in 1958 with a small array of silicon cells as backup power; it has been in orbit for over 65 years and is the oldest man-made object still in space, its primary batteries having died in 1964 while its solar-powered transmitters continued briefly — a testament to the longevity of photovoltaic power.

The modern skateboard evolved from homemade wooden boards with roller-skate wheels attached, first appearing in California around 1950; the first commercial skateboards were sold in 1958 by Roller Derby, and the invention of urethane wheels by Frank Nasworthy in 1972 transformed skateboarding from a dangerous novelty into a serious sport.

The electron was discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897 during experiments with cathode ray tubes; by measuring the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles, he proved they were lighter than atoms and universal components of all matter, fundamentally changing our understanding of atomic structure and earning him the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics.

The modern hearing loop (induction loop) that lets hearing aids and cochlear implants receive a wireless audio signal in theaters and public spaces was invented by Joseph Poliakoff in 1937; despite being over 80 years old, the technology is still the most widely installed assistive listening system in Europe, found in ticket offices, churches, and airports.

The modern safety helmet for motorcyclists was invented by neurosurgeon Hugh Cairns in 1941 after he witnessed T.E. Lawrence (Lawrence of Arabia) die from a motorcycle head injury; Cairns's research on head injuries led to the mandatory use of helmets by British military motorcyclists during WWII, saving hundreds of lives.

The first video game console for home use was the Magnavox Odyssey, designed by Ralph Baer and released in 1972; Baer had the idea in 1966 while waiting for a colleague in a bus terminal and sketched out a 'TV game' concept; Atari's Pong (1972) was directly inspired by an Odyssey tennis game, leading to a landmark patent lawsuit that Magnavox won.

The first wearable computer was the Osborne 1, released in 1981 by Adam Osborne; weighing 24 pounds and the size of a sewing machine, it was marketed as 'portable' and came with bundled software — a revolutionary business model — selling 125,000 units before Osborne Computer famously went bankrupt in 1983 after pre-announcing a successor model, killing its own sales.

The artificial limb dates to ancient Egypt, where a functional prosthetic big toe found on a mummy dates to around 950–710 BCE; it is made of wood and leather and shows evidence of wear, suggesting it was used in life, not just placed with the body for religious reasons — making it the world's oldest known functional prosthetic device.

The jackhammer drill was key to building the Panama Canal; the US engineers used pneumatic rock drills to excavate over 200 million cubic yards of earth and rock between 1904 and 1914, a project that also required invention of improved dynamite blasting techniques, steam shovels, and sophisticated disease-control programs to combat malaria and yellow fever.

The Post-it note's distinctive yellow color was not intentional — it was simply the color of scrap paper lying next to Art Fry's workstation when he first tested Spencer Silver's adhesive; 3M later discovered through consumer research that yellow was actually preferred by users because it looked informal and temporary, and yellow became the standard.

The paper bag with a flat bottom was invented by Margaret Knight in 1870, allowing bags to stand upright and hold much more than the earlier envelope-style bags; a man named Charles Annan stole her design, but she sued him and won when she produced her original drawings and models as evidence — becoming one of the first women to win a patent dispute against a man.

The modern disposable contact lens was introduced by 1-800-Contacts and Johnson & Johnson with the Acuvue brand in 1987; the concept of daily disposable lenses (thrown away after one day) was invented by Danish ophthalmologist Michael Bay in 1987, reducing the risk of eye infections dramatically compared to monthly or extended-wear lenses.

The modern syringe with a plunger was independently invented in 1853 by Scottish physician Alexander Wood and French surgeon Charles Pravaz; Wood is credited with developing the hollow needle combined with the plunger barrel, and his first use was injecting morphine to treat nerve pain — though he used it so liberally he became dependent on the drug himself.

source.name: Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh

text: Instant noodles were invented by Momofuku Ando in 1958 in a small shed behind his house in Osaka, Japan; Ando wanted to create a convenient meal using surplus wheat flour donated by the US after WWII, and after months of experimenting he discovered that flash-frying noodles created a dry product that could be rehydrated quickly in hot water — Nissin's Chicken Ramen became Japan's first instant noodle product.

The MP3 audio format was developed by a team at the Fraunhofer Society in Germany led by Karlheinz Brandenburg, who spent years perfecting a psychoacoustic model that removed inaudible frequencies; the format was standardized in 1991 and, when the first portable MP3 player (the MPMan) went on sale in 1997, it triggered a music industry revolution and the rise of digital piracy.

The first programmable electronic digital computer designed in the US, ENIAC, weighed 30 tons and filled an entire room, using 18,000 vacuum tubes that required over 150 kilowatts of power; it ran so hot that the building's temperature rose significantly when it was in operation, and the vacuum tubes burned out at a rate of about one every two days.

The escalator motor design inspired the 'people mover' or moving walkway, first used at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago; later implemented at airports, the moving walkway allows travelers to cover long terminal distances faster — Charles Richter's 1954 Richter patent for an airport moving walkway created the standard design still used in most airports today.

The pogo stick was invented by George Hansburg in 1919, who brought it from Germany to the US after encountering a toy for a German girl named Pogo; Max and Ernst Pohlig originally invented it in 1920 with a spring mechanism, and Hansburg licensed the American rights, then improved the design — early pogo sticks were made of wood that swelled in moisture.

The latex rubber glove was introduced in surgery by William Halsted at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1894, initially to protect his scrub nurse Caroline Hampton's hands from the carbolic acid used for disinfection — not for sterility; after Halsted married Hampton, he pushed for their universal use, and rubber gloves became a standard of sterile surgical technique.

The modern crossbow was invented in China around 450 BCE, significantly earlier than the longbow's peak development in medieval Europe; the Chinese repeating crossbow (zhuge nu) could fire up to 10 bolts in 15 seconds, making it arguably the world's first semi-automatic weapon, and it was still in military use in China as late as the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894.

The pop-top aluminum can was introduced by the Pittsburgh Brewing Company in 1962 and rapidly adopted by the beverage industry; the shift from steel to aluminum cans in the 1970s was driven not by chemistry but economics — aluminum can be recycled indefinitely without quality loss, and today recycled aluminum supplies about 73% of all new aluminum can production.

The cochlear implant was developed by Australian physician Graeme Clark, who had been inspired as a student by his father's deafness; the first multi-channel cochlear implant was implanted in Rod Saunders in 1978 in Melbourne, and over 700,000 cochlear implants have since been fitted worldwide — though the device remains controversial within some deaf communities.

The polio vaccine was developed by Jonas Salk, who announced his inactivated poliovirus vaccine in 1953 and field-tested it on 1.8 million children in 1954 — the largest medical trial in history at that time; when trials were declared a success in April 1955, church bells rang across America and Salk was treated as a national hero, yet he never patented the vaccine.

The modern steel-frame skyscraper was enabled by the invention of Bessemer steel and the development of the internal steel skeleton by engineer William Le Baron Jenney; his Home Insurance Building in Chicago (1885), using a partial steel frame, is considered the first skyscraper, and the technique allowed buildings to rise far higher than masonry construction permitted.

The programmable thermostat for home heating was patented by Warren Johnson in 1883, but the first commercially successful electronic programmable thermostat for homes, the Honeywell T8000, was introduced in 1985; the Nest Learning Thermostat, introduced by Tony Fadell and Matt Rogers in 2011, marked the beginning of the smart home era by learning residents' schedules automatically.

The mechanical television camera was invented by Paul Nipkow in 1884, using a rotating disk with holes to scan an image; while mechanical television was eventually superseded by electronic systems, Nipkow's disk concept is still used in confocal microscopes and laser scanning systems used in scientific imaging today.

The first synthetic antibiotic, Salvarsan (arsphenamine), was discovered by Paul Ehrlich in 1909 after 605 failed compounds in his search for a 'magic bullet' that would kill bacteria without harming the patient; compound 606 worked against syphilis, and Ehrlich's systematic approach to drug discovery became the foundation of modern pharmaceutical research.

The modern bicycle derailleur gear system was patented by Paul de Vivie (pen name Vélocio) and other French cyclists in the early 1900s, allowing bikes to climb hills more easily; early Tour de France rules banned derailleurs as cheating, and it was not until 1937 that the Tour de France allowed derailleurs in competition.

The modern thermostat was invented by Warren Johnson in 1883 and first used to control building temperatures at Milwaukee Downer College; the bimetallic strip thermostat — which uses the differential expansion rates of two bonded metals to open or close a circuit — was patented by Albert Butz in 1886 and remains the mechanism in many simple home thermostats today.

The first photographic film was invented by George Eastman, who coated paper with a gelatin silver bromide emulsion in 1884 and developed the Kodak camera in 1888; the camera came pre-loaded with enough film for 100 exposures, the user mailed it back to Kodak for processing, and Eastman's advertising slogan 'You press the button, we do the rest' democratized photography.

The AK-47 assault rifle was designed by Mikhail Kalashnikov in 1947, a Soviet tank mechanic who developed it after being wounded in WWII and hearing soldiers complain about their weapons; the rifle's simple design with loose tolerances made it incredibly reliable in muddy, sandy, and extreme temperature conditions, and an estimated 100 million have been produced worldwide.

The Venn diagram was created by English logician John Venn in 1880 as a tool to illustrate logical relationships between sets using overlapping circles; while the basic concept was used earlier by Leonhard Euler, Venn formalized and popularized it in his 1880 paper 'On the Diagrammatic and Mechanical Representation of Propositions and Reasonings.'

The EpiPen auto-injector was developed from military injectors designed to allow soldiers to administer antidotes to nerve agents in the field; Sheldon Kaplan, an engineer at Survival Technology Inc., adapted the design in the late 1970s for epinephrine delivery in anaphylaxis emergencies, and it received FDA approval in 1987.

The modern padlock was invented in ancient China, and by Roman times sophisticated padlocks with spring-bolt mechanisms were in use throughout the empire; the mass-produced padlock was invented by Harry Soref, who founded Master Lock Company in 1921 using laminated steel construction — his first lock was so strong he demonstrated it by shooting it with a bullet.

The television remote control was invented by Zenith Radio Corporation's Eugene Polley in 1955 as the 'Flash-Matic' — a flashlight that triggered photocells on the TV corners to change channels; a later ultrasonic remote by Zenith's Robert Adler became more common, and the infrared remote dominant today was patented by Paul Hrivnak in 1974.

The spork (combined spoon-fork utensil) was patented by Samuel W. Francis in 1874, though the word 'spork' was trademarked by the Hyde Company in 1909; while modern culture associates the spork with fast food, it was originally marketed for elegant dining as a 'practical' utensil for certain foods that needed both scooping and piercing.

The nuclear power plant was pioneered by the Experimental Breeder Reactor I (EBR-I) in Idaho, which on December 20, 1951, became the first power plant to generate usable electricity from nuclear fission, producing enough power to light four light bulbs; the first full-scale commercial nuclear power station was Calder Hall in England, opened in 1956.

Liquid paper (correction fluid) was invented by Bette Nesmith Graham, a secretary in Dallas who mixed tempera paint in her kitchen blender and used it to paint over typing errors; she patented Liquid Paper in 1958 and built the company from her kitchen, eventually selling it to Gillette for $47.5 million in 1979; she was also the mother of Monkees member Mike Nesmith.

The smoke jumper parachutist firefighter program was developed by the US Forest Service in 1940 as a way to rapidly deploy firefighters to remote wilderness fires; the first operational jump was made by Rufus Robinson and Earl Cooley in Nez Perce National Forest, Idaho, on July 12, 1940, demonstrating that parachutes could be used for civilian emergency services.

The first synthetic fiber, rayon, was developed by French chemist Hilaire de Chardonnet in 1884 as an alternative to silk; he called it 'artificial silk' and demonstrated it at the 1889 Paris Exposition — the same year the Eiffel Tower was unveiled — and his factory launched the world's first synthetic fiber industry in Besançon.

The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by Alexander Fleming on September 28, 1928, when he returned from vacation to find a mold (Penicillium notatum) had contaminated a petri dish and killed the surrounding bacteria; Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed it into a usable medicine in 1940, and the three shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The parking garage was invented along with the automobile; the first multi-story parking garage in the US was built in Boston in 1898, initially called a 'motor stable,' designed to accommodate the wealthy early car owners who needed secure indoor storage; by 1929 there were over 3,000 garages in the US and the term 'parking' had entered common usage.

The VCR (video cassette recorder) came to market as a format war between Sony's Betamax (1975) and JVC's VHS (1976); despite Betamax being technically superior in video quality, VHS won because it offered longer recording times (allowing users to record full movies) and was licensed to more manufacturers at lower cost, establishing an important lesson in technology adoption.

The DNA double helix structure was discovered by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953 at Cambridge, building crucially on X-ray crystallography data produced by Rosalind Franklin (Photo 51); Franklin's contribution was not fully acknowledged during her lifetime — she died in 1958 before Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1962.

The pager (beeper) was invented by Al Gross, who also invented the walkie-talkie and the cordless phone; Gross patented the pager in 1949 and it was first used at New York City's Jewish Hospital in 1950; the pager reached peak usage in the mid-1990s with over 60 million users in the US before being rapidly displaced by the cell phone.

The Hubble Space Telescope was launched by the Space Shuttle Discovery on April 24, 1990; embarrassingly, a flaw in its primary mirror was discovered afterward, and the telescope's images were blurry until astronauts on STS-61 installed corrective optics in 1993 — the repair mission became one of the most celebrated achievements in NASA history.

The air traffic control system began in the US in 1935 when airlines established the first Airway Traffic Control station in Newark, New Jersey; the first formal air traffic controller was Archie League, who guided aircraft using colored flags and an umbrella for shade at the St. Louis airport in 1929, managing traffic on a chalkboard.

The first music recording made for public sale was a wax cylinder recorded by Austrian soprano Ginevra de Bagnoli for Edison's company in 1889; the first recording made by a Black artist for commercial release was George W. Johnson's 'The Whistling Coon' in 1890, and he reportedly hand-cranked a phonograph to make 500 individual copies per day.

The breathalyzer was invented by Robert Frank Borkenstein of the Indiana State Police in 1954, replacing the earlier 'Drunkometer' invented by Rolla Harger in 1938; Borkenstein's device used a photometric colorimetric reaction where alcohol in breath caused a color change in potassium dichromate solution, and it became the standard for drunk-driving enforcement worldwide.

The GIF (Graphics Interchange Format) was invented by Steve Wilhite at CompuServe in 1987 to reduce the size of color images for transmission over slow modems; the format supports animation through multiple frames, a feature not originally intended to become its defining use — and Wilhite sparked a cultural debate in 2013 when he insisted the correct pronunciation is 'JIF' with a soft G.

The power drill was invented by Arthur James Arnot and William Blanch Brain in 1889 in Australia for use in mining; the first portable electric hand drill for general use was invented by Wilhelm Fein of Stuttgart, Germany, in 1895; the Black & Decker pistol-grip trigger-switch portable drill, patented in 1917, became the model for virtually all subsequent hand drills.

The first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier, USS Enterprise (CVN-65), was commissioned in 1961; it used eight reactors and could travel without refueling for over 20 years, and its commissioning represented a revolution in naval power-projection capability — the ship served until 2017, a service life of 51 years.

The microSD card, introduced in 2005 by SanDisk (as TransFlash before being standardized), is the world's smallest mass-produced data storage device at 15×11×1mm; despite its size, modern microSD cards can store up to 2 terabytes — equivalent to about 400,000 photos — demonstrating one of the most dramatic examples of Moore's Law in consumer products.

The automatic rice cooker was invented by Yoshitada Minami, an engineer at Toshiba, in 1955; before its introduction, Japanese housewives had to monitor boiling rice continuously; the early electric cooker used a simple bimetallic thermostat and transformed Japanese domestic life, and today Japan sells more rice cookers per capita than any other country.

The modern steel-tipped plow was invented by John Deere in 1837, who discovered that highly polished steel could cut through sticky Midwestern prairie soil that clogged existing cast-iron plows; Deere's invention enabled the cultivation of the Great Plains and transformed the American Midwest into the world's most productive agricultural region.

The inkjet printer was invented by multiple researchers independently in the late 1970s; Hewlett-Packard's thermal inkjet technology (1979) used a tiny heating element to vaporize ink into a bubble that sprayed a droplet, while Canon simultaneously developed a similar 'BubbleJet' system; the first consumer inkjet printer, the HP ThinkJet, was released in 1984.

The automated assembly robot was first installed in a factory by General Motors in 1961; the Unimate robot arm, designed by Joseph Engelberger and George Devol, worked the night shift at a GM plant in New Jersey, extracting die castings from machines and welding them — it never took a sick day and was one of the first steps in industrial automation.

The ice cream cone was popularized at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair when an ice cream vendor reportedly ran out of dishes and a nearby waffle vendor started rolling his waffles into cone shapes; several people claim credit for the invention, but Ernest Hamwi, a Syrian waffle vendor, is most often cited as the person who spontaneously adapted his waffles into cones.

The first programmable industrial loom in the modern sense was the Northrop loom, invented by James Northrop in 1895; it automatically replaced empty bobbins without stopping the weaving process, increasing productivity so dramatically that one weaver could tend 24 Northrop looms versus 2 ordinary looms — causing massive unemployment in the British weaving industry.

The modern disposable coffee cup with a corrugated sleeve was invented by Jay Sorensen in 1991 after he spilled hot coffee on himself; the Java Jacket sleeve he invented allowed customers to hold hot cups without burning their hands, reducing the need for double-cupping, and is now used on billions of cups annually worldwide.

The bionic prosthetic arm with mind control was first demonstrated by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory's Modular Prosthetic Limb in 2010; the arm responds to nerve signals in the residual limb or chest muscles, allowing amputees to perform complex tasks including individual finger movements — representing the convergence of neuroscience, robotics, and materials science.

The laser printer was invented by Gary Starkweather at Xerox PARC in 1969, who modified a Xerox copier to accept computer data and print it using a laser beam; Xerox released the first commercial laser printer, the Xerox 9700, in 1977, and HP's LaserJet (1984) made laser printing affordable for offices, transforming business document production.

The first transatlantic telephone call was made on January 7, 1927, between London and New York using radio wave transmission; it cost $75 for a three-minute call (equivalent to about $1,200 today), and only one conversation could take place at a time in each direction — yet it was enormously popular, with over 11,000 calls placed in the first year.

The Segway's balancing technology uses five gyroscopic sensors and two tilt sensors to make 100 balance corrections per second; while the Segway itself was commercially disappointing as a transportation device, its self-balancing platform technology inspired the development of hoverboards, self-balancing unicycles, and modern delivery robots.

The electric eel inspired the battery; Alessandro Volta invented the Voltaic pile (first battery) in 1800 after corresponding with Luigi Galvani about the animal electricity in frogs' legs, and Volta explicitly named the unit of electrical potential ('volt') after himself — though it was the electric eel that first demonstrated to naturalists that living organisms could generate electricity.

The first commercially successful electric car was not a 21st-century invention — it was the 1884 Thomas Parker Electric Car built in Wolverhampton, England; in 1900, electric vehicles outnumbered gasoline-powered cars in the US, and it was only the discovery of cheap Texas oil in 1901 and Ford's assembly-line Model T that made gasoline cars dominant.

The Geiger counter was invented by Hans Geiger and Walther Müller at the University of Kiel in 1928; the device detects ionizing radiation by counting electrical pulses created when radiation passes through a gas-filled tube — Geiger had previously collaborated with Ernest Rutherford on the experiment that discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911.

The pressure cooker was invented by French physicist Denis Papin in 1679, who called it the 'steam digester'; Papin demonstrated it to the Royal Society in London and even cooked a meal for King Charles II — but when he tried to bring a large steam pressure vessel onto the Thames, he was stopped by the boatmen's guild, who feared it would put ferrymen out of work.

The first successful helicopter with a counter-rotating coaxial design was built by Coaxial Designs pioneer Igor Sikorsky, but the first person to achieve sustained helicopter flight was Paul Cornu in France on November 13, 1907, hovering about 1 foot off the ground for 20 seconds; practical helicopters required decades more engineering to achieve stable, controllable flight.

The first digital watch was the Hamilton Pulsar Time Computer, introduced in 1972 at a price of $2,100 ($15,000 today); it used LEDs to display the time only when a button was pressed to conserve battery, and it was immediately worn by celebrities including Roger Moore's James Bond character — helping to make it a status symbol before affordable quartz watches disrupted the market.

The fire hydrant was invented in the US in the early 19th century, but its specific inventor is unknown because the patents office and most documents were destroyed in the great fire of 1836; Frederick Graff Sr. of Philadelphia is often credited with inventing the modern fire hydrant around 1801, and Philadelphia is known as the birthplace of the municipal water supply system.

The personal computer graphical user interface (GUI) was developed at Xerox PARC in 1973 with the Alto workstation, which used a mouse, windows, and icons; Apple's Steve Jobs visited PARC in 1979 and was so impressed he immediately directed his teams to incorporate those concepts into the Apple Lisa (1983) and then the Macintosh (1984).

Cheeseburgers were first served in 1924 by 16-year-old Lionel Sternberger at his father's Pasadena, California sandwich shop, though the exact origin is disputed; the term 'cheeseburger' was trademarked by Louis Ballast of the Humpty Dumpty Drive-In in Denver in 1935, and the fast-food cheeseburger was standardized by McDonald's in the 1950s.

The crash helmet for motorsports was first systematically advocated by Hugh Cairns, the British neurosurgeon who had treated T.E. Lawrence's fatal head injuries; his 1941 paper in the British Medical Journal arguing for mandatory helmets for motorcyclists directly influenced military adoption, but mandatory motorcycle helmet laws for civilians in the UK did not come until 1973.

The ballistic vest made from Kevlar was first developed for law enforcement use by the National Institute of Justice in the early 1970s; the Threat Level I vest was first worn in service by Seattle police officer Ray Glivar in 1975, and by 2006, the NIJ estimated that soft body armor had saved the lives of more than 3,000 US police officers.

The blender was invented by Stephen Poplawski in 1922, who designed a device with a spinning blade at the bottom of a container, initially to make malted milk drinks; Fred Waring, a popular bandleader, invested in a redesigned version in 1936 and promoted it extensively — the 'Waring Blendor' became the first blender widely sold to the public.

The photographic negative was invented by William Henry Fox Talbot in 1835 as the 'calotype' process, using silver salts on paper; while Daguerre's daguerreotype (1839) produced a sharper image, Talbot's negative-positive process allowed unlimited copies to be made from one negative — this fundamental principle of photography remained standard until the digital era.

The elevator safety brake invented by Elisha Otis in 1852 made skyscrapers possible; before his invention, a broken rope meant a deadly plunge — Otis's spring-loaded 'guide rail' mechanism would grip the shaft walls if the rope broke; the invention is often cited as one of the key enabling technologies of the modern city alongside steel and the internal combustion engine.

The compact fluorescent light bulb (CFL) replaced the incandescent in many markets, but LEDs have now largely displaced CFLs in turn; the LED's efficacy has improved from about 20 lumens per watt in 2000 to over 200 lumens per watt in 2023, making it over 10 times more efficient than an incandescent and 4 times more efficient than a CFL.

The patent system itself was invented in Venice in 1474, when the Venetian Senate passed the world's first patent statute; the law gave inventors a 10-year exclusive right to use their inventions in exchange for public disclosure, establishing the core bargain of modern patent law: the state grants a temporary monopoly in exchange for public knowledge.

The QWERTY keyboard was standardized in the 1870s by Christopher Latham Sholes, but the competing Dvorak Simplified Keyboard, designed by August Dvorak in 1936, places the most commonly used letters on the home row and is believed by its proponents to be faster; despite decades of study, evidence that Dvorak is faster remains inconclusive, and QWERTY persists through sheer lock-in.

The espresso machine was invented by Angelo Moriondo of Turin, Italy, who received a patent in 1884 for a large industrial machine capable of making coffee rapidly using steam pressure; Luigi Bezzera improved the design in 1901 to create individual servings under 9 bars of pressure — the standard for modern espresso — and sold his patents to Desiderio Pavoni.

The modern credit scoring system (FICO score) was introduced by Fair, Isaac and Company in 1989, though the company had developed credit scoring models since the late 1950s; the three-digit FICO score from 300–850 is now used in over 90% of US lending decisions, and Bill Fair and Earl Isaac, its inventors, based it on statistical analysis of consumer payment histories.

The game of basketball was invented by Canadian physical education instructor James Naismith in December 1891 at the YMCA International Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts; tasked with creating an indoor winter sport, he nailed peach baskets to a 10-foot elevated track and wrote 13 basic rules — the game was first played with a soccer ball.

The game of volleyball was invented in 1895 by William Morgan, physical director of the YMCA in Holyoke, Massachusetts, who wanted a game for older businessmen less strenuous than basketball; he called it 'Mintonette,' and the name 'volleyball' was coined when an observer described the act of volleying the ball back and forth over the net.

The first commercial video game was Computer Space, created by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney in 1971, which was based on the space combat game Spacewar!; while commercially unsuccessful due to its complex controls, it led Bushnell and Dabney to found Atari in 1972 and create Pong — the first commercially successful video arcade game.

The modern crossword was adapted for the digital age in 1996 when The New York Times became the first major newspaper to offer interactive crosswords online; the digital crossword spawned apps like the NYT Crossword (2018) which reached over 1 million subscribers, proving that a 110-year-old puzzle format could thrive in the smartphone era.

The refrigerated railcar was invented by J.B. Sutherland of Detroit in 1867, who patented a design using ice packed at either end with air circulation through slatted floors; Gustavus Swift worked with engineer Andrew Chase to develop the first successful commercial refrigerator car in 1877, allowing fresh beef from Chicago slaughterhouses to reach Eastern cities.

The walkie-talkie was invented by Al Gross in 1938 and first used by Canadian Army units in WWII; the first practical battlefield 2-way radio, the SCR-536 'Handie-Talkie' developed by Motorola engineer Dan Noble in 1940, was light enough to carry with one hand and became essential for coordinating infantry movements, transforming military communications.

The Fourdrinier paper machine was patented by brothers Sealy and Henry Fourdrinier in 1806, based on a design by Nicholas Louis Robert; the machine could produce paper in a continuous roll rather than individual sheets and reduced papermaking from a skilled handcraft to a mechanized process, enabling the mass-production of newspapers and books.

The electric blanket was first patented by the American physician Sidney Russell in 1912 as a 'thermo-electric blanket' for tuberculosis sanatoriums; the first mass-market electric blanket for domestic use was introduced by Simmons Company in 1946 after the technology was refined during WWII for aviators' heated suits.

Styrofoam (extruded polystyrene foam) was invented by Ray McIntire at Dow Chemical in 1941 while trying to develop a flexible electrical insulator; the material was 30 times lighter than regular polystyrene and provided excellent thermal insulation, and it was first used to make life rafts for the US Coast Guard during WWII.

The mechanical pencil was invented by Sampson Mordan and John Isaac Hawkins in England in 1822; early models pushed thin lead (graphite) rods through the tip by twisting the barrel; the first retractable mechanical pencil was patented by Charles Keeran in 1915, and the EVERSHARP brand became so popular that 'eversharp' temporarily became a generic term.

The weather satellite was pioneered by TIROS-1 (Television Infrared Observation Satellite), launched by NASA on April 1, 1960; it transmitted the first TV pictures from space of Earth's cloud cover and proved that satellite technology could improve weather forecasting; modern weather satellites provide data that has made 5-day forecasts as accurate as 1-day forecasts were in the 1980s.

The Holga camera was invented by T.M. Lee in Hong Kong in 1982 as an inexpensive plastic camera for the mass market; despite (or because of) its light leaks, lens vignetting, and soft focus, it became a cult object among art photographers who prized its unpredictable results, leading to the 'lomography' movement and demonstrating that 'defects' can become desirable features.

The modern diving regulator was invented by the French engineer Émile Gagnan and Jacques-Yves Cousteau in 1943, adapting an automobile gas demand valve to deliver air at ambient pressure on each breath; the invention made self-contained diving practical and eventually spawned an enormous recreational scuba diving industry.

The printed circuit board (PCB) was invented by Austrian-British engineer Paul Eisler in 1936 while working in London; he printed conductive pathways on an insulating board, replacing hand-wired circuits, and the US military used his technology in proximity fuses during WWII — though Eisler received very little financial benefit from the invention.

The seatbelt as a three-point harness was invented by Nils Bohlin at Volvo in 1959, who designed it after working on aircraft ejection seat safety; Volvo made the life-saving decision to give the patent away for free, allowing all car manufacturers to use it — a choice that has been credited with saving over one million lives.

The first aerosol spray can was patented by Erik Rotheim in Norway in 1927 using a mixture of propellant and liquid product; Lyle Goodhue and William Sullivan refined the concept in 1941 to produce the 'bug bomb' for the US military, and after WWII the technology was adapted for consumer products ranging from hairspray to whipped cream.

The fluorescent light tube was invented by Peter Cooper Hewitt in 1901, and the modern fluorescent lamp was developed at General Electric in 1934 by a team including George Inman; the first public demonstration was at the 1939 World's Fair in New York, and by 1951 fluorescent tubes produced more light in the US than incandescent bulbs.

Bluetooth wireless technology was named after Harald Bluetooth, a 10th-century Danish king who famously unified warring Danish tribes; engineers at Ericsson invented the short-range radio standard in 1994, naming it 'Bluetooth' as a code name to denote unifying different communication protocols — the Bluetooth logo combines Harald's initials in runic script.

The modern piano's iron frame was invented by Alpheus Babcock in 1825, allowing strings to be stretched at much higher tensions than wooden frames permitted; this single innovation enabled the modern grand piano's rich, powerful sound, and today a concert grand's combined string tension is approximately 20 tons — requiring an iron frame to hold it safely.

The post-it note adhesive used in Post-it Notes is technically a microencapsulated adhesive that forms tiny spheres that make only partial contact with surfaces; each sphere-shaped bubble of adhesive is about 0.5 millimeters in diameter, and the reason the note repositions cleanly is that these tiny spheres can only weakly bond, then cleanly release and rebond to new surfaces.

The tape measure was patented by Alvin Fellows in 1868; it used a spring-return mechanism so the tape retracted automatically when released, the same basic mechanism in nearly all tape measures today; before standardized tape measures, carpenters' rules varied between craftsmen and regions, making standardized construction nearly impossible.

text: The drone (unmanned aerial vehicle) for military use traces back to the Kettering Bug, an early aerial torpedo developed in 1918 by Charles Kettering for the US Army — a wire-guided, gyroscopically stabilized aircraft designed to fly into targets; modern military drones evolved from reconnaissance aircraft and became widely used for surveillance and strikes from the early 2000s onward.

The caterpillar track was patented by Richard Edgeworth in 1770, but the first practical application was Benjamin Holt's steam-powered agricultural tractor in 1904 — a Holt factory foreman reportedly described how it 'crawls along like a caterpillar'; tanks using the Holt design were first deployed by the British Army at the Battle of the Somme in 1916.

The Pap smear test was developed by Georgios Papanicolaou, a Greek-American physician, who described the test in 1928; after initially being ignored by the medical community, the technique was widely adopted after a 1943 publication, and by reducing cervical cancer deaths by over 70% in the US since the 1950s it is considered one of the most successful cancer-screening tools ever developed.

The first fiber-optic endoscope for looking inside the human body was developed by Basil Hirschowitz at the University of Michigan in 1957, allowing doctors to visually examine the stomach without surgery; modern endoscopes with video cameras and tools for biopsy allow minimally invasive procedures that have replaced many surgeries that would previously have required large incisions.

The ball bearing was likely used in Roman ships at Lake Nemi in the 1st century BCE, but the modern precision ball bearing was invented by Welsh inventor Philip Vaughan in 1794; the roller bearing was patented by John Harrison (the clockmaker who solved the longitude problem) in 1761, though it was never published during his lifetime.

The modern power grid traces its origins to the War of Currents between Thomas Edison (DC) and Nikola Tesla/George Westinghouse (AC) in the late 1880s; AC power won because it could be transmitted over long distances using transformers to step voltage up and down, while Edison's DC systems required a power station every mile — the 1893 Niagara Falls power project sealed AC's victory.

The self-adhesive postage stamp (the kind that doesn't require licking) was first issued by Sierra Leone in 1964, though the technology was patented earlier; the US Postal Service introduced self-adhesive stamps in 1974, discontinued them due to adhesive problems, and permanently switched to them in 1993 — now over 90% of all US stamps are self-adhesive.

The mechanical spring was used in locks in ancient Egypt, but the coiled spring (spiral spring) was described by clockmaker Petrus Heinlein in Nuremberg around 1510 and enabled the development of portable clocks and watches; Robert Hooke published the law of spring elasticity (Hooke's Law) in 1678, which describes the linear relationship between force and extension.

The first commercially successful synthetic paint (alkyd resin oil paint) was developed by Roy H. Kienle at General Electric in 1926; alkyd paint dried faster than traditional linseed oil paints and was more durable, and it became the standard in household and industrial painting — though it has been largely replaced in consumer markets by water-based latex paints since the 1950s.

The safety bicycle lock was invented in the late 19th century, but the modern U-lock was designed by Michael Zane in 1972 to counter the bolt cutters that could easily defeat chain locks; the hardened steel U-shape resisted cutting tools and became the gold standard for urban bicycle security — though even U-locks can be defeated by an angle grinder in seconds.

The first practical submarine was the Turtle, built by David Bushnell in 1775 for the American Revolution; operated by Sergeant Ezra Lee in 1776, it attempted to attach a mine to the British warship HMS Eagle in New York Harbor — the first ever submarine military attack — but failed to penetrate the ship's copper-sheathed hull.

The assembly line concept predates Ford; the meat packing industry in Cincinnati in the 1830s used a 'disassembly line' where pigs were moved on overhead rails past workers who each performed one task; Ransom Olds used a moving-chassis assembly line at Oldsmobile in 1901, twelve years before Ford's Highland Park factory — though Ford's implementation was faster and more systematic.

The modern football (soccer ball) was standardized when the Football Association in England adopted rules requiring a spherical ball in 1863; the first machine-stitched football was produced by Mitre Sports in 1872, and the iconic black-and-white Telstar ball (named for its resemblance to a communications satellite) was introduced for the 1970 FIFA World Cup in Mexico.

The vacuum tube (thermionic valve) was invented by John Ambrose Fleming in 1904 and improved by Lee de Forest in 1906 with the addition of a control grid; de Forest's triode could amplify electrical signals and became the foundation of radio broadcasting, early computers, and all electronics until transistors replaced them in the 1950s.

The modern flush urinal was patented by Andrew Rankin in 1866, though simple urinals had existed for centuries; the waterless urinal, using a trap with floating liquid that seals odors without water, was invented by Klaus Reichardt in 1991 and can save up to 40,000 gallons of water per unit per year compared to flush urinals.

The first practical typewriter with the SHIFT key — allowing one machine to type both upper and lower case letters — was invented by Byron Brooks in 1872; before the shift key, typewriters required separate keys for capitals and lowercase, effectively doubling the keyboard size; the shift key's adoption made typewriters compact enough for office use.
